Mr. Herter will arrive on the morning of Saturday, July 11, and will leave for Geneva later the same day.

speakeroldname: Hon. Raymond O'Hurley (Minister of Defence Production):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the outset I would refer you to the actual content of our estimates for the current fiscal year. It will be noted that more or less substantial increases are shown over the estimates for 1958-59 for five of the items, and a decrease in one. Only vote 71, which provides for payment of grants in lieu of taxes on crown owned defence plants operated by private contractors, remains relatively unchanged. In addition, the main estimates include one new item, vote 72, and another new item of major importance appears as vote 504 in the supplementary estimates.
I would like to explain briefly these changes and innovations. Vote 68, which provides for the costs of departmental administration, shows an increase of roughly $275,000 or 4 per cent over the provision made in 1958-59. The bulk of the increase is accounted for by salaries and is attributable to normal annual increments and some upgrading of positions. Those factors have been offset to some extent by a reduction in the total establishment from 1,527 positions to 1,509 positions. I might add that this will be the seventh successive year in which both the authorized establishment and the actual number employed have been reduced.
It will be noted that a further increase amounting to $41,500 is included in the supplementary estimates under vote 502. This is designed to provide for increased travel which has been made necessary largely by departmental activities relating to Canadian-United States production sharing.
Vote 69, for the care, maintenance and custody of stand-by defence plants, buildings, machine tools and production tooling, has also been increased from $450,000 to $882,000. There will actually be a decrease for the second successive year in the amount budgeted for care and custody of defence plants in stand-by condition. However, the task of preserving and storing or disposing of crown owned machine tools and tooling has assumed much larger proportions as a result of the completion of programs for the production of the CF-100, Sabre and T-33 aircraft, and the termination of the Arrow and Iroquois programs.
Vote 70 provides a total of $2,907,000 for capital assistance, which represents an increase of $807,000 over the provision made last year. In fact the provision for capital works and equipment accounts for only $1,657,000 of the amount requested under this vote. The remaining $1,250,000 represents a new departure, related to our efforts to increase the participation of Canadian industry

in United States defence programs under the production sharing plan. In many cases in which Canadian manufacturers might be interested in competing with United States firms for such business, an American firm may enjoy a substantial advantage because most of his preproduction and tooling costs have already been written off under previous contracts. The object of the proposed provision, therefore, is to offset his relative advantage, in part at least, by absorbing a portion of the relevant preproduction and tooling costs in Canada.
I would add that this provision is related, in our minds, to the first year or two of production sharing, when Canadian industry must frequently break into production programs which are relatively well established in the United States. During that period we shall be able to judge the effectiveness of this type of assistance, and determine whether or not it would be appropriate or necessary in subsequent years.
Vote 72 is a new item in the estimates this year and it will be noted that vote 503 in the supplementary estimates provides an additional $450,000, bringing the total requested for the year to $950,000. The purpose of these votes is to make funds available to establish Canadian sources of electronic component parts essential to expected Canadian military requirements. The needs of forthcoming equipment programs can be met in this country only if action is taken in anticipation of these programs to tool up industry for production and obtain production samples which will meet military standards. Limited action has been taken along these lines in past years, using funds available to the Department of National Defence for the development of electronic components; however, it was decided this year to place the development of qualified production sources on a more systematic basis, and to include the necessary funds in the estimates of my department.
This is of necessity a selective program in which we must weigh each case in the light of the quantities of the components likely to be required and existing manufacturing capabilities on which we can build. For approved projects, the funds are intended to cover such costs as production engineering, tooling, the manufacture of sample components, test equipment and testing, evaluation for qualification approval, training and cost studies. It is expected that most of this money will be spent on a fairly wide range of projects, each of them involving only a relatively small amount. I might add that while the purpose of this provision, as originally conceived, is to establish sources of components related to Canadian military 66968-9-359i
Supply-Defence Production requirements, the establishment of such sources also assists Canadian industry in its bidding for United States orders.
Vote 73, which provides for the expenses incurred by Defence Construction (1951) Limited in procuring the construction of defence projects on behalf of the Department of National Defence, shows an increase of about $340,000 or 11 per cent over 1958-59. This reflects the expectation that total defence construction expenditures will be almost double those for last year, taking into account the construction of new Pine Tree stations, Bomarc launching sites and the Sage station. Despite this large increase in the program the expected increase in personnel, which is the chief reason for the additional funds, amounts to only about 15 per cent.
Vote 74, for the administration and operation of Canadian Arsenals Limited, shows an increase of $200,000 over 1958-59. For some years prior to last year the volume of sales achieved by this company was sufficient to cover all its operating costs. Last year, however, sales declined to the point where it became necessary to revert to the practice of the post world war II period and appropriate funds to cover the deficits of the arsenals. A further reduction in the volume of sales is expected in the current year, and the gap between anticipated revenue and costs is therefore widened.
On the other hand vote 75, which provides for the cost of construction, improvements and new equipment for Canadian Arsenals Limited, is further reduced this year by the amount of $226,000. The vote covers only capital costs of a general nature and excludes amounts attributable to specific programs; the latter would be covered by vote 70.
Finally I would direct your attention to vote 504 in the supplementary estimates, which asks for $5 million and commitment authority for an additional $4 million to support selected defence development programs. This item is closely related to the production sharing program and owes its origin to the same circumstances which gave rise to that program. As long as Canada was undertaking the independent development and production of the major equipment requirements of the armed forces, Canadian industry was able to build up and maintain sizeable engineering teams and to develop an advanced technology in a number of fields. As it becomes increasingly difficult for Canada to develop major weapon systems independently, the support previously given to development engineering by the equipment programs of the Canadian services is lessened. We are therefore taking

Supply-Defence Production other steps to ensure that existing engineering capacity will be maintained to the greatest extent practical, and that our technological progress will not be impeded.
This is important for many reasons, among them being the serious effect which a decline in Canadian engineering capabilities would have on our production sharing efforts. The weapon systems and equipments which seem to offer the greatest promise for future production sharing are all characterized by a very high degree of engineering content. Canadian industry will be able to share in such production programs only if its engineering capacity can be maintained and its technical competence advanced through the performance of appropriate development tasks. I would emphasize that we are determined that any Canadian role under production sharing should include some of the more demanding work and not be limited to the pouring of concrete or to what is often called "metal bashing".
The choice of projects to be financed from this vote will, of necessity, be restricted to the most promising areas of development, and no attempt will be made to cover the whole field. We must obviously consider the ability of Canadian industry to meet the engineering demands of particular projects. We must also estimate the prospects for future production orders, which will require a forecast of the future requirements of both the United States and Canadian forces. In addition, the development program will be worked out in a long term context to ensure the greatest possible continuity and stability of Canadian industrial engineering. It will also take account of the probable industrial needs of the civilian economy, to which certain lines of technological advantage may be especially relevant.
The method of selecting and administering development projects is being worked out in consultation between my department and the departments of finance and national defence. There will also be continuous consultation with the United States agencies responsible for defence research and development.
I must point out that there is an element of risk in all development projects. Nobody knows for certain in advance whether the expenditures of development funds will produce a piece of hardware acceptable to the armed forces. There are bound to be failures, and this risk will have to be accepted. Even the failures, however, are likely to be offset in part by the technical experience gained by the industrial teams involved. For those projects which are successful, of course, there is every expectation,

taking into account the much larger United States requirements, that substantial production orders will result.
(Translation):
Those are the main changes and innovations provided this year in the estimates of this department. The remainder of my introductory remarks will deal with some of the most important aspects of our current activities and with the progress made in respect of the production sharing plan.
During the last fiscal year, expenditures for purchases and construction were hardly lower than in former years. The net value of new contracts and of changes in previous contracts is but only slightly higher than the figure for 1957-58. During the current year, I am not expecting any great difference in the degree of our activities, based on the value of contracts and the amount of expenditures.
However, statistics do not give any indication of the main change which has occurred and which is still being developed in the nature of our work. This change, the setting up of a production sharing scheme between Canada and the United States, follows the important decisions taken during the last year with regard to our defence program. As parliament and the people in general soon recognized, these decisions have shown the growing complexity of modern weapons and the ever more complete integration of Canadian-American continental defence arrangements which make it extremely difficult for our country to undertake alone the development and production of the main weapons.
The government had realized the situation more than a year ago. It was obvious that programs like that of the Bomarc missile and the SAGE system, which were being considered at the time, and also the possibility of other more remote defence programs against ballistic missiles, would require a reorientation of the larger part of our development and of our defence production in Canada. Instead of confining ourselves to the sole requirements of Canadian armed_ forces, we would have to get more and more together with the United States, and co-operate with them. In theory, these arrangements were provided for in the Hyde Park agreements and the statement of policy of 1950 with regard to economic co-operation. But, this general theory of co-operation had to be put into practice so that it would apply to the new circumstances. This was the origin of the production sharing plan.

Hon. members will remember that on February 23 last, I informed them of the steps we had taken up to that day jointly with the American authorities for the purpose of an actual sharing of production. I may say that we have resorted to every possible means. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) first of all raised the matter during his last summer's talks with president Eisenhower. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Pearkes) and myself have explained Canada's point of view to the defence secretary of the United States on various occasions, namely at the meeting of the joint Canadian-American defence board last December. We also exchanged correspondence with Mr. McElroy and the late Mr. Quarles, of the American defence department, in which we dealt with general policy but also pointed out Canada's interests with regard to specific equipment requirements in the United States. Officials of both countries, among whom were my deputy minister and the deputy minister of national defence, took part and will again take part in a number of talks in order to direct and accelerate the implementation of the program. Various working groups, consisting of Canadian and United States officials responsible for special aspects of the program, are meeting almost continually.
(Text):
At an early stage in our discussions with the United States authorities we were able to get their agreement to a definition of the objectives of production sharing. As I reported to the house last February 23, we set ourselves an immediate aim of increasing the participation of Canadian industry in the production and support of North American defence weapons; we also adopted a continuing objective which recognizes the long term nature of the problem with which we were faced, and looks to the co-ordination of the defence requirements, development, production and procurement of the two countries in order to achieve the best use of their respective production resources for their common defence.
In pursuit of these objectives two broad courses of action appear to be appropriate for the Department of Defence Production. The first is to obtain United States recognition and acceptance of Canadian sources of supply. This had to begin, of course, at the top, at the secretarial level in the United States and among the assistant secretaries responsible for the procurement programs of the three services.
It is here, of course, to the senior United States authorities that we have had to look for the removal or modification of policies and
Supply-Defence Production regulations which would hamper Canadian industry's participation in United States procurement programs. The most important example of action of this kind, which I reported to the house on May 1, was the revision of the "buy American" regulations. The general effect of these changes was, of course, to waive the "buy American" act in respect of purchases in Canada of the main kinds of defence equipment within the capabilities of Canadian industry.
There are other instances of action at the secretarial level to remove impediments. Duty free entry, for example, has always been a problem in the past, but arrangements are being worked out for this privilege to be extended to imports of Canadian defence material. I might explain that the exclusion of duty from a Canadian bid for evaluation purposes, under the waiver of the "buy American" policy, does not in itself provide for duty exemption when the material actually enters the United States, unless a duty free entry certificate has been granted. The problem has, in the past, been felt chiefly at the subcontract level, which will, we hope, be an important area of future Canadian sales. I am now confident that the problem will be remedied.
A further problem related to security restrictions. Most of the important defence programs in the United States carry a security classification, which has often had the effect in the past of excluding Canadian firms from access to these programs. A "need to know" could not be established for Canadian industry chiefly because the Canadian forces had no requirement for the equipment in question. The United States authorities are very strict, and understandably so, in their insistence on a "need to know", and even their own industries are unable to obtain information about projects in which they are not directly involved. Now, however, in most cases the production sharing program has been accepted as sufficient grounds for the removal of this security bar, whenever Canadian firms are interested in projects for which their capabilities may be appropriate. Canadian industry is therefore finding it easier to discuss with the large defence contractors in the United States many of the important programs in which the latter are engaged.
By actions such as these we have obtained a framework of United States policy and regulations which is favourable to Canadian participation. But this is only the first step toward securing acceptance of Canadian sources. Many of the actual procurement decisions in which Canadian industry might be interested are taken at the lower levels of the

Supply-Defence Production United States armed service departments, often at procurement centres far removed from Washington, and by the prime contractors or even subcontractors. It has been necessary, therefore, to embark on a broad program of making United States procurement offices and contractors aware both of the implications of the new policies and regulations of their own government and the capabilities of Canadian industry.
In terms of the man-hours of Canadian officials, this has been and will continue to be a major concern of my department in the production sharing program. We have reinforced the staff of our Washington office which, as the Leader of the Opposition observed a short time ago, can play a vital liaison role with the United States authorities. We have stationed officers at key United States project offices. Other officials have been assigned for as long as six months at a time, to work with United States contractors in an effort to discover and bring to their attention opportunities for Canadian participation. The major United States contractors have also been supplied by my department with detailed reports of Canadian production facilities which could be employed on their projects.
I might say that the United States authorities have recognized the need to make their production sharing policy effective at the level of their procurement offices and contractors, and have supported us generously in our efforts.
We have from the outset enlisted Canadian manufacturers to help in this task of education, and representatives of a number of our industries have visited Washington and major United States procurement centres, both to help us in familiarizing United States authorities with Canadian capabilities and to be briefed by those authorities on United States procurement programs and procedures. A growing number of Canadian firms have also acted individually, sending their representatives to visit contractors throughout the United States. I should like to emphasize that this kind of action-the face to face meeting between Canadian and United States industry-is essential to the success of production sharing.
For the same reason, United States contractors have been encouraged to visit Canada and obtain first-hand knowledge of Canadian facilities. I might add that in doing this we have been confident that Canadian industry would make an impressive showing, and this has, in fact, been the experience to date. Our Canadian capabilities are neither as large nor as broad as those of our great neighbour, but within the limits of

specialization Canadian defence industry is the equal of any in its physical plant and manufacturing skills.
All this, then, constitutes one of our lines of attack, going after United States acceptance of production sharing, and recognition of the contribution which Canadian industry can make. The other line of approach has been to help Canadian industry to exploit the opportunities which the production sharing program may present.
I might emphasize at this point that we can only try to help. We have consistently taken the view, in our own procurement program, that the interests of both the Canadian taxpayer and the armed forces are best served when manufacturers compete for our contracts. I can assure the committee that the United States authorities are no less insistent on this point in their procurement programs, and that Canadian firms who are seeking United States defence orders are entering a highly competitive field. In some cases the competition will be largely a matter of price; in others the technical aspects of proposals may be of equal or even greater importance. I know, however, that Canadian manufacturers are aware of this. I am confident that they will go after United States orders aggressively, and will bring all their skills and imagination to bear in the framing of their proposals. If they are not prepared to make this effort, nothing my department can do will make the production sharing program work.
On the other hand I realize that there are ways in which government can help, and we are pursuing these courses as energetically as possible. We are anxious, in the first place, to advise Canadian firms on what is involved in doing business with United States defence agencies and contractors, and to help them to identify the programs in which they might take part. We have prepared and distributed a brochure explaining United States procurement regulations and practices, in which we have tried to include all the information which is necessary to a firm seeking United States orders. As I have indicated, we have arranged for many companies to attend briefings in the United States. We have welcomed inquiries from interested Canadian firms, and I might at this point renew our offer of advice and assistance.
Both the department and the Canadian Commercial Corporation are undertaking to keep abreast of United States requirements, in order to draw to the attention of Canadian firms any opportunities which are likely to be of interest to them. As a result of these efforts, and especially as Canadian industry establishes its own direct links with United

States procurement offices and contractors, there should be no opportunities missed through lack of knowledge.
In addition to the foregoing, there are other more tangible ways in which we may be able to help. I have already outlined two of these in my explanation of the items in the main and supplementary estimates. Vote 70, in part, offers some assistance to Canadian companies who may find themselves competing with United States companies who have already written off most of the tooling and preproduction expenses on previous orders. Vote 504, as I have explained, represents a far-reaching effort to ensure that Canadian skills are kept abreast of developments in defence technology, so that our industry can play its proper role in future production programs.
In addition, mention might be made of the reserve of crown owned machinery which is held by the department. This has been available to Canadian industry over the years to be used on Canadian defence production programs. In some cases items from the reserve might appropriately be made available to Canadian companies wishing to enter into United States defence contracts or subcontracts, providing, of course, that they already have the basic facilities and skills needed for the job.
In summary, I can say without hesitation that production sharing has overshadowed in importance all other concerns of my department in the past year, and will continue in the current year to have first claim on my own attention and that of my senior officials and a large number of officers of the department.
To this point, I have been reporting on what my department was doing, and what it intended to do, to promote production sharing. I feel that this is information which the committee, and the public at large would want and are entitled to have. I realize, however, that in the last analysis it is the results which count.
Firm figures for United States purchases in Canada during the first half of 1959 are not yet available. I may say, however, that during this period United States government procurement offices have placed prime defence contracts in Canada to the value of approximately $32 million. This figure covers Canadian manufactured military equipment only, and does not include construction, maintenance and service contracts. The comparable figure for the first six months of 1958 was $17 million. There has therefore been an increase of $15 million or 90 per cent in direct United States government orders alone. Moreover, within these totals the proportion
Supply-Defence Production representing more complex types of equipment has increased and for the first six months of this year accounted for two-thirds of the total direct orders. Since the end of June we have learned of the award of further contracts, valued at over $3 million, for advanced electronic equipment.
To this must be added the value of subcontracts placed in Canada as a result of the combined efforts of my department and Canadian industry to interest United States prime contractors in Canadian sources of supply. Over 100 such orders have been received, with an aggregate value in excess of $20 million. Many of these orders have a significance far beyond their relatively modest value, since it is a common practice of United States contractors to order small quantities for evaluation with the intention of placing substantial follow-on orders if these initial deliveries are satisfactory.
Too much should not be read into these figures. The idea of production sharing is too new and our experience is too limited to permit any very definite conclusions to be drawn. I am satisfied, however, that the initial results justify optimism on our part.
In the remainder of my statement I propose to review the principal sectors of our current production program and the status of the industries involved. In the field of aircraft production, the major government programs in which the industry is now engaged involve the CP-107 Argus maritime reconnaissance aircraft, the CC-106 transport version of this, the CS2F or tracker anti-submarine aircraft and the CC-109 cosmopolitan transport. The order for the Argus will, however, be completed late this year, and a number of subcontractors have already been affected. The CS2F will be completed in early I960. The effect will be felt by subcontractors several months earlier, but subcontract orders in connection with the Albatross rescue aircraft will provide a partial replacement.
Work on the two transport aircraft will continue for a longer period, and there are now grounds for hoping for substantial commercial orders for both of these. As the committee will be aware, Canadair have already received orders for 15 of the commercial version of the CC-106, with options for the sale of 10 more. Since then other carriers have shown an interest both in this aircraft and their CL-540, which is the transport known to the air force as the CC-109. Needless to say I welcome the initiative shown by the company in stimulating commercial interest in these aircraft, both of which owe their existence to the support given by the government.
Sales of the Beaver and Otter utility aircraft are also continuing, and the Caribou,

Supply-Defence Production which seems likely to satisfy a substantial United States government requirement, is being further developed. The de Havilland Company of Canada has, of course, established a well deserved, world wide reputation as a designer and manufacturer of utility aircraft.
Aero engine production in Canada is now concentrated on supporting the Orenda engines which will continue, for several years, to be employed in large numbers by both the R.C.A.F. and a number of foreign air forces, the manufacture of the 1820-82 piston engine for the CS2F and the Albatross, and the production of Pratt and Whitney piston engines and parts for the world wide market. The repair and overhaul program will, of course, continue to provide steady employment in all sections of the industry, to provide with only a slight falling off as older types of aircraft are replaced.
The sum total of all these programs does not, of course, provide a work load which will support the existing aircraft industry. We therefore attach considerable importance to production sharing in this area and welcome such orders as those which have already been received relative to the Bomarc missile program.
For the same reason, the announcement that the F-104G has been selected as a replacement for the Sabre aircraft in the air division will be of enormous interest to the industry. It is obviously and understandably of great interest to this committee, and although a great deal of hard work remains to be done before contracts are signed I can at least report today on the action we propose to take in the procurement of this aircraft and the kind of program we expect to have.
In view of the fact that we have three major aircraft manufacturers in Canada, each of which is capable of undertaking this program, it has been decided to award the main contract on the basis of competition, in which each of the three will be invited to submit proposals. Whatever may be the outcome of this competition, it is certain that the program will create a substantial volume of work for the Canadian aircraft and associated industries over the next three years. The total cost of the program over this period will run to over $400 million, and at its peak it will create employment for approximately 10,000 people, of whom something over 5,000 will be required by the prime airframe and engine contractors. This work will, of course, be distributed widely throughout industry as a result of subcontracting.
The airframe will be manufactured in Canada with the exception of a small number of parts. Moreover, it is our expectation, based on discussions with Lockheed, that our purchases in the United States of the remainder

of the airframe components will be oifset by the assignment to Canada of the production of certain airframe sections for the requirements of Germany. For the production of the J-79 engines for these aircraft we are now beginning negotiations with Orenda Engines Limited. It is the opinion of the government that this firm is the most suitable for this work, providing their costs can be kept strictly within reasonable limits, and we are looking to the determination of a firm price.
As in the case of the airframes, these engines will be manufactured in Canada except for a hard core of parts for which tooling costs would be prohibitive in a requirement of this size. Here again our imports of engine parts will be offset by other component purchases in Canada by the United States manufacturers. In other words, both for the airframe and the engine the principle of production sharing has been fully accepted by the United States firms involved.
We are now working toward a similar understanding with the developers and manufacturers of the fire control and flight control equipment required for this aircraft. Until these discussions have proceeded further I would hesitate to forecast the actual production program which the Canadian electronics industry will be called on to undertake. I can say definitely, however, that the greater part of this work will be done in Canada, including a number of tasks which will be of a challenging character and consequently of importance for the preservation of the industry's engineering capabilities.
I might give the committee some idea of the expected impact of this program on future budgets, about which the Leader of the Opposition asked last Saturday. In the current year expenditures will be relatively slight, amounting to only about $6 million. In 1960-61 this will be multiplied almost tenfold, the present estimate being $57 million. In 1961-62 this in turn will be roughly doubled, and the peak will be reached the following year when an estimated $120 million will be spent, assuming current price levels and wage rates. Expenditures will fall slightly in 1963-64, during which year the program will be completed, and thereafter only relatively minor expenditures will be required for final settlements.
A breakdown of costs based on the principal elements of the program may indicate its probable impact on Canadian industry. About 41 per cent of the estimated cost of an F-104G, in fly-away condition, represents the airframe. The engine accounts for about 23 per cent, instruments and flight equipment

for 16 per cent and electronic equipment, including the fire control system, for 13 per cent. The remaining 7 per cent represents payments to the original manufacturers for Canada's share of the design and engineering costs associated with the "G" model of the F-104, together with the licence fee and royalties. The engineering charges which I mentioned provide for engineering the airframe to take the fire control system, and strengthening the wings. These costs will be shared equally with Germany, and the Canadian share will be further reduced if the aircraft is adopted by other countries.
I would emphasize that all the cost and expenditure figures and percentages I have given are simply the best estimates we are able to make on the basis of our production studies and preliminary discussions with the Lockheed company. The actual contractual terms remain to be settled by negotiation. I might add that since the decision was announced last week, my officials have met with representatives of Avro, Canadair and de Havilland to explain to them the basis on which proposals are to be submitted, and it is our intention that the prime contractor shall be chosen, on the basis of the proposals received, within six weeks from now.
Interest has also been expressed in the basis on which prices are to be established. This too, of course, remains to be settled by negotiation, but I can assure the committee that we shall not contract on any cost-plus formula. For some items it may be possible to negotiate firm prices from the outset, but in the main the plan is to start on the basis of target prices, with incentive features. Where this is done we shall subsequently negotiate firm prices as soon as our experience with production costs permits.
The Leader of the Opposition asked last Saturday whether provision would be made for alteration of the terms if there were to be a change in our NATO commitments. I can only say that any changes in the requirement, short of cancellation, will be dealt with by the normal procedure for amending contracts, and that each contract will contain the usual provisions relating to cancellation.
As the Minister of National Defence indicated last week, the first of these aircraft will be delivered early in 1961, about 18 months after the contract is awarded. I might add to this, in response to a question by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, that thereafter the delivery rate will build up to a monthly rate of 10 aircraft, reaching this in six or seven months. Deliveries will continue at this rate until completion of the order by mid-1963. Peak employment under this schedule will be reached early in 1961. We are
Supply-Defence Production anxious to get on with this program with the least possible delay, and I can assure the committee that my department will undertake the many negotiations involved with the utmost speed consistent with protecting the taxpayers' interests.
I turn now from the aircraft program to the electronics program. The electronics industry differs from the aircraft industry in that it serves three separate major markets with widely divergent requirements. Defence electronics is just one of these, the other two being the large consumer market for radio and television products and the growing market for industrial applications of electronics. Experience has shown, however, that defence electronics has set the pace of engineering in the industry and has produced the developments on which the growth of the other two markets has rested. The future health of the industry rests largely on the degree to which it is able to participate in future defence programs and, in this way, maintain and develop its engineering skills.
The growing integration of our defence forces with those of the United States probably has a greater effect on this industry than on any other, since the electronics content is particularly high in those weapon systems which form the basis of that integration. We are therefore now in a transition period, which is likely to persist for two or three years, during which Canadian defence electronics production must be reoriented, in a very large measure, to serve a North American rather than a Canadian market.
There is no reason to believe that the general level of activity in defence electronics in this country should decline in the foreseeable future, since the equipment plans of our armed forces, as well as those of the United States, continue to place a growing emphasis on electronics applications. There are also encouraging signs that the Canadian industry, as it showed at the recent meeting of its association, is beginning to adjust itself to the new defence environment, and some initial successes have been achieved in the radar, data processing and communications fields in competition with United States firms.
The other sectors of the defence production program, while they reflect the same changes in defence strategy and establishments, offer fewer opportunities for production sharing.

The shipbuilding program will continue at approximately its present level, which is substantially below the peak of the Korean and post-Korean period. The one major new project to be started in the current year involves a fleet tanker to support the destroyer escorts. It has been decided to invite tenders from Canadian shipyards for the construction of this ship. The original order for 14 destroyer escorts will be completed during the current year. Work has now started on the first of the six additional destroyer escorts, which will be similar to H.M.C.S. Restigouche in all essential respects, and the second ship will be begun in the very near future.
While there is a continuing need for weapons and ammunition of conventional patterns, production in these categories is expected to decline further during the current year. New types of weapons may offer some opportunities for the industries which were engaged in this kind of work, but these are likely to be limited by the radical differences in the nature of the new equipment and the relatively small numbers in which they are required.
In summary, it might be said that the defence production program and the industrial complex associated with it are now going through a process of adjustment, reflecting the changing character of modern defence and the increasing integration of Canadian and United States continental defence forces which has resulted from this fundamental change. I am satisfied that the nature of this adjustment is now well understood by the civilian and military authorities and the defence industry in both Canada and the United States. We are determined that the resources of this country shall continue to play an effective role in the new circumstances, and with the co-operation which we are receiving both from our own military authorities and from the procurement agencies and contractors in the United States, I am confident that this can be done.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the minister for his very comprehensive statement in introducing his estimates in the house. I do not intend to deal with the technical questions which have been raised in his statement but I presume that some of my colleagues, far more competent than I am, will have a few words to say about this subject.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I found that the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) devoted
[The Chairman.]

a considerable part of his speech to what he called the contract sharing scheme or plan between Canada and the United States in the defence field.
I shall naturally have something to say in the matter a little later on in my remarks, but, for the present, I want to deal with some extraordinary powers that are conferred upon the minister. I want to mention those powers, Mr. Chairman, because, before 1957, then hon. members who are occupying today government benches and who were sitting then on this side of the house frequently said that the Minister of Defence Production had extraordinary powers, so extraordinary that they could even shake up this country's whole economy. According to them, it was due, of course, to the manner in which the minister was using his statutory powers.
Mr. Chairman, I only want to give two or three instances of those extraordinary powers. According to paragraph (e) of subsection 1, section 17 of the act:
A contract may be entered into by the Minister without the approval of the Governor in Council if
(i)	in the opinion of the Minister, the contract must be entered into immediately in the interests of defence,
(ii)	the estimated expenditure, loan or guarantee does not exceed twenty-five thousand dollars, or
(iii)	competitive tenders have been obtained and the lowest tender, involving an estimated expenditure not exceeding fifty thousand dollars, is accepted; but the Minister shall make a report to the Governor in Council in respect of any contract involving an estimated expenditure, loan or guarantee exceeding ten thousand dollars and entered into without the approval of the Governor in Council.
A little further on in the act, Mr. Chairman, we find section 23, and I would like to quote the first subsection:
Where a person who has been requested to enter into a defence contract on terms and conditions that the Minister considers to be fair and reasonable has refused or failed to enter into the contract, if the Minister is satisfied that such person owns or controls facilities that are suitable for or can be adapted to the work required to carry out such contract and that his refusal or failure was without reasonable excuse, the Minister may direct that person to produce, deliver or store, or to construct, as the case may be, on such terms and conditions and within such period as the Minister considers to be fair and reasonable in the circumstances, the defence supplies or the defence project or projects that would have been the subject-matter of the contract if it had been entered into.
In concluding my remarks with regard to the extraordinary powers conferred upon the minister under the Defence Production Act, I would like to quote subsection 2 of section 27. To my mind, Mr. Chairman, that

clause embodies one of the most extensive powers conferred upon the minister under the act. It reads as follows:
Where a controller has been appointed to carry on a business or a part thereof, he shall be deemed to be the agent of the owner thereof for the purpose of carrying on the business or that part thereof, except that the owner shall not have any right to control the business or that part thereof and the controller may, subject to any instructions of the minister, do all such things as he thinks fit for the purpose of carrying on the business or that part thereof.
Mr. Chairman, nothing would be simpler than to quote other sections of the act and point to the extraordinary character of the powers conferred upon the minister under that act. If I felt I had to deal briefly with the matter it is because, as I pointed out at the beginning of my remarks, some members who were formerly in the opposition and who are now ministers have vigorously denounced those extraordinary powers conferred by the act upon the Minister of Defence Production.

The minister, however, has indicated in his statement that he is very hopeful that current developments and discussions with our United States colleagues will lead to some improvement. I most sincerely hope so.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking to these estimates one feels like a tenant raising cain with the charwoman instead of going to see the landlord. Of course in this instance it is difficult to know who the landlord is. Sometimes I think it is the Minister of National Defence, sometimes the Secretary of State for External Affairs and sometimes I suspect that the lord of the manor is somewhere down in Washington. It is difficult to know how far to go in this department. It is rather obvious that the minister has little to do with the policies that determine the expenditures.
The point raised by the speaker who preceded me largely had to do with what the "ins" said when they were out. One point the hon. gentleman did not deal with was the difference in personality between the previous minister of defence production and the present minister. We are all aware of the image that was built up of the former minister of this department. He was made out to be a rather fearsome ogre and perhaps merited all the attacks about the powers given him under certain legislation. The fact that these attacks have led to no consequential change is not so much because the present government is perfidious and is not true to its former stand but because under our form of government power tends to build up around a personality or an individual. I think we should look at other departments of this government and see
Supply-Defence Production where that is happening. Fortunately the present minister is not an ogre. I see one minister sitting on the front benches who may be an ogre, but that has nothing to do with these estimates.
In our section of the country we have an example of an industry that is badly in need of defence production orders. This raises a question of the dilemma which confronts the government in its purchasing policy in so far as defence industries are concerned. Over the years defence industries like all others have tended to be concentrated in certain areas of the country and specifically in what might be called the golden triangle from Windsor to Sudbury to Montreal. This concentration has been accelerated in the last 10 years by the fact that most defence industry production is notable for its high capital input and a lessening of its labour input.
This concentration seems to revolve around the fact that in defence purchasing we are getting more and more complicated articles involving more and more engineering skill, as the minister pointed out. This naturally has led to an increased concentration of defence production purchases in the highly industrialized regions. It has meant that the much smaller areas like the lakehead have fallen behind. Perhaps in the natural justice of things these areas should fall behind because they cannot compete in certain terms due to higher transportation costs and the like with the more highly concentrated parts of the country.
In Port Arthur we have an important industry that enjoyed a good reputation for production in the past. In the last few years the company has not been able to obtain substantial orders to make it an important or basic aircraft supplier for the government.
