I should like to make a general reference to defence production policy with reference to one very narrow sector and one specific industry, namely the Canadian Car Company plant in Fort William. This plant had a record in the last war of producing aircraft. Since the last war it has had some aircraft contracts and it also produced buses. Recently, it moved into the field of trailer production. In other words, we had an amalgam of commercial production and defence production. Not too long ago the company came under the control of the

Supply-Defence Production great industrial-certainly defence production-giant of A. V. Roe. It is another example of the kind of concentration of industry that I was speaking about earlier. Not too long after A. V. Roe took over this company it was announced that the Canadian Car plant would move its commercial operations to Montreal where there was a new, or a newer, plant than they had in Fort William, and that unless there were some defence orders forthcoming the plant at the lakehead would close. The reaction of the community was immediate and to my mind it is the kind of reaction that raises questions about damn fool socialism and damn fool capitalism. Here we have the spectacle of an entire community, labour unions, municipal officials, rotary club and other service clubs, practically every organization in the community, off touting for defence contracts for this particular company.
When the company made the statement that it was uneconomical to go on with commercial operations in this particular plant and that on the grounds of corporate realism they must move to Montreal, they immediately, of course, brought to the fore the question, what about defence production orders in the same plant? Would they not be too high cost? If the same factors are at work in commercial production, surely they are at work in defence production, and so you have the dilemma that the local people were shilling -if you want to use a slang term-with the government for defence production orders to keep this plant going. And yet if the economic justification for the commercial transfer is true, then the adequacy of this plant for defence production orders on the basis of pure efficiency and the cheapest defence products of the best standard at the best price was obviously, or to me obviously, ruled out.
So you had the spectacle of this very large -well, the largest corporate structure perhaps in Canada-A. V. Roe Company, having the community doing its leg work, one might say, and putting pressure on this particular government in order to get a defence contract that would keep the plant open. In fact, in the past the company did indicate that if there were substantial defence orders, it might reconsider their commercial orders. In fact, what has happened is that the commercial production either has been or is in the process of being switched, and so our only hope of keeping that plant open is to have a substantial order.
The minister is aware that the order that the government has-I will not say promised -given every indication of giving to Fort William is the production of the Bobcat, the armoured fighting vehicle of the army, that the Minister of National Defence referred to.

This particular vehicle is in the development stage. Ostensibly, or conceivably, if it passes the development test and it fits into government policy, then the government will go ahead and decide to place an order, and if the company puts in any kind of decent bid that order will go to Fort William and so we will keep our plant alive and over a thousand people in employment terms and a much larger number in terms of population of the community will be pleased. But, as I said when I first introduced this topic, there is a question of principle here and a fine opportunity for the government to enunciate a policy.
I pointed out earlier there has been this tremendous concentration in a golden triangle. It is a triangle that happens to fit into the United States concentration and beyond this particular region it is very difficult for secondary industries to get going. In the main they often have to be sustained by some form of government contract. While we can regret this concentration, yet it certainly is a fact that it exists and I think that it is a fact the government has to take into consideration in its purchasing policy. If what I see across the country in all the places outside of this particular triangle, and one or two other isolated major industrial regions in Canada, is true, we have a problem which is much larger than the lakehead problem.
Wherever you go in Canada, outside of the very large areas, you hear this bleat or this call for secondary industries. Every part of the country wants secondary industries. The people realize that the primary industries they may have such as pulp and paper, transportation, and such things, are not substantial enough to give them the kind of development they dream of. Therefore, when you go into northern Ontario, around Timmins or around Sudbury, or when you go into Manitoba and into eastern Quebec, or into any of these regions you hear the talk always, "We want and we need secondary industries". It seems to me that here would be an opportunity for this government in its defence procurement policy to recognize this particular need and to deliberately-that is by deliberate policy- decide to react from the concentration in the highly industrialized regions and deliberately direct their defence procurement policy in giving this type of secondary industry, if it is a type of secondary industry, to the regions and the communities that do not have them at present or are losing out at present.
I could give another example at the lake-head where we are finding that our shipyard cannot pick up orders to compete, and there again we are up against a situation. I certainly hear this, "Oh, would that we had

C. D. Howe around again; C. D. would throw us a ship or two to sort of keep us going". My reference to Mr. Howe is not a derogatory one. I just want to make the point that this sort of thing should not be done from the point of view of largess. An order should not come into Fort William just because we are in desperate need; it should come because there is a government policy to direct this kind of contract and this kind of work to areas that are not taking part and have not taken part in this tremendous concentration of industry. To me, this is one of the ways that this government could indicate by such a policy that it has a long range plan for the economy as a whole. I do not think it has to be ashamed of having a long range plan, if it has one up its sleeve.
The very sobering realization came to me the other day, after looking at a study by an economist on the location of the iron and steel industry in Canada, that most of the dreams of places like Fort William and Port Arthur about eventually having some kind of integrated steel operation are dreams that are never going to come to fruition within the next two or three decades unless there is some completely unusual technical change. This particular thesis argued that the plant of Dosco in Nova Scotia, for example, is uneconomical and that its future can only be guaranteed by different forms of government subsidy.
We have had a number of examples in the house of the kind of subsidy that affects that particular operation. We have had examples in the house countless numbers of times, if you check back over the last few decades, where measures have been brought in that recognize, for example, that the western farming community has problems that require a government policy which will direct and assist them down the line. I suggest to the minister that in the field of defence procurement there is a possibility for a government policy that will really help the smaller communities outside the industrial concentrations to develop or to keep alive secondary industry without the opprobium of being looked upon as inefficient or incapable of competing with the much larger scale organizations that are possible in the Montreal and Toronto areas. It seems to me that this possibility would be an antidote to what the former member for Port Arthur and great cabinet minister, if you wish, in the last government, advocated. It seems to me that his policy of getting things done during the war and in the years immediately after the war, arising from the impetuous nature of the man, was of real worth in
Supply-Defence Production terms of war effort but it left out the question of over-all planning and it showed very little consideration of the long term aspects of support for secondary industries or the development of secondary industries in those regions outside the triangle.
It is not within the minister's competence at the present time to enunciate such a policy but I think his department is one area where such a policy can very easily come forward. There are many members of the house who come from communities not unlike the one I represent and who have this very real problem. I imagine that someone who comes from a region embracing some of the smaller cities in the Ottawa valley or some of the smaller communities outside of Montreal or from such places as Halifax and Sydney must be very much aware of this problem and the real possibility of government leadership in this field with the blanket recognition and acceptance by most of the people of Canada, I believe, that here is a situation where straight economic efficiency in terms of the cheapest possible product in the shortest possible time is not necessarily the most important factor.
The final point I want to touch on in relation to the Department of Defence Production is the question of United States orders and the possibilities of Canadian firms getting in on them. Again, in the case of the region from which I come we have the example of rumour and counter-rumour to the effect that the industry involved there has not even been trying to get United States orders. I know that the minister can probably scotch that story and I hope he will do so later during the discussion of his estimates. I think we would appreciate having from him at some stage during his estimates a brief statement about the position of aircraft parts suppliers in this country, with specific names mentioned, and what are the possibilities of the groups in Edmonton, Winnipeg, the lakehead and in other parts of the country aside from the big three to whom he referred who I imagine are Canadair, de Havilland and Avro. I should ask the minister to be frank in his exposition. I think these places would appreciate knowing what is likely to happen rather than to have some golden hope hung in the air which they are not going to be able to reach. If the minister would do that I think it would enable me and the hon. member for Fort William to clear up some misapprehensions that exist in our area, and I would hope he would do the same for the others.
I cannot end my remarks without saying that throughout the past year I have appreciated the pleasant and informative way in

Supply-Defence Production which the minister, his deputy and their associates have always come forward with as much information as they possibly could when they were asked, and in that regard I have no complaints at all about this department. That situation is quite in contrast to that in the Department of Transport and the Department of National Defence. Before you rule me out of order, Mr. Chairman, I want to say that I have never had a straight answer from the Department of National Defence. I should like to suggest to the Minister of National Defence that with regard to sending out letters if he wants to see in operation a technique of giving straight answers he should drop over and have a chat with the Minister of Defence Production or his deputy. He might then be able to improve one very minor aspect of his public relations.

Mr. Chairman, I have a
couple of specific matters I should like to deal with but before doing so may I commend the minister on the activity of his department in opening the way for Canadian industry to participate in defence production contracts originating in the United States and also with regard to the success the department has had in getting rid of the buy American act from the point of view of defence sharing.
At one time Vancouver was a major airplane manufacturing centre. During the war the Boeing Aircraft Company had large plants on Sea island and produced many planes. It is not a remarkable fact that the majority of the aircraft manufacturing plants in the United States are on the west coast because the physical facilities in regard to airplane manufacturing require rather massive, high structures with very large door openings and such structures are more readily, easily and cheaply built on the west coast where you do not have winters such as occur in the east to contend with. After the war these facilities were absorbed by the overhaul plants of Canadian Pacific Air Lines and Trans-Canada Air Lines.
The previous speaker referred to the decentralization of industry and it seems to me that the major manufacturing complex which is in existence on the west coast is a logical place for an airplane manufacturing industry. It follows the pattern set in the United States, and we have had past experience in that form of manufacturing. We have the skills and the technicians out there to carry it on. We know that Avro, Canadair and de Havilland are the three major manufacturing plants and, to refer only to Avro and Canadair, it would seem to me that they were set up in Toronto and Montreal respectively because the majority of their work was


government work and therefore they located in areas that were fairly close to Ottawa so that they would have quick and easy contact with government officials and with the government itself. I believe that we have passed beyond that phase, at least I hope we have, although we do have a saying out on the west coast that we may be 3,000 miles away by air but we are 300,000 miles away as a matter of actual fact.
I would suggest to the minister it is about time that some particular study was given to the problem of spreading out defence contracts across Canada and in particular, so far as I am concerned, to the west coast. I would suggest a team of experts from the department might well visit the west coast and become acquainted with what can be done there. They might have discussions with existing manufacturers on the west coast, including Fairey Aviation and the Bristol Company, who know a fair amount about building airplanes. They could ascertain whether or not a few of these defence contracts in connection with certain phases of airplane building, perhaps also in the electronics field, might be placed with established manufacturers on the west coast.
In general, the procurement of the Department of Defence Production does tend to centre around the manufacturing heartland of Canada in Ontario and Quebec. This is understandable because again the great bulk of manufacturing is concentrated there, and also it is very easy for the representatives of such manufacturers to visit Ottawa and gain information as to what is required. They are in a preferred position so far as being in touch with what is coming up is concerned. Not too long ago I had an instance of this in connection with the construction of radar towers. We have a firm in Vancouver that could build these towers and they were asked by Canadian Commercial Corporation, I believe, to bid on this contract. However, by the time the firm got the information there was not enough time left to prepare a bid. Furthermore, representatives of the firm would have to visit United States defence officials in New York in order to be briefed on the particular requirements. It was just impossible for this firm to compete because of their distance from Ottawa. I think the fact that we happen to be 2,500 or 3,000 miles away from Ottawa should not be an insuperable barrier to our participation in contracts from the Department of Defence Production.
I feel it is up to the department, not the individual manufacturer, to do something to bring the west coast manufacturer into a position where he can complete on an equal

basis, so far as information and engineering advice is concerned, with his eastern counterpart. 1 would suggest, as I said before, that the area around Vancouver is an ideal area for participation in this F-104G project. Instead of limiting participation to Canadair and Avro or de Havilland I suggest we might consider Bristol or Fairey or some other company on the west coast in order to distribute some of the procurement for defence more equitably across the country. We do participate now in the construction of ships for national defence, but that is the only place where we get what I consider to be a fair break.
There is one other point I should like to make, and that is in connection with the calling of tenders for supplies for the armed forces. The air force has three delivery points, Moncton, Edmonton and Weston, Ontario. Moncton is for eastern Canada; Edmonton for western Canada and Weston, Ontario, for central Canada. In regard to navy procurement, the delivery is to various stores depots, but for the army a manufacturer invariably has to quote a price delivered to the central depot at Cobourg. Since freight is sometimes a major item in building up costs, and since you do not quote an f.o.b. factory price but f.o.b. the stores point, this makes it difficult for west coast manufacturers. Even if these stores delivered to Cobourg have to be sent to depots in Calgary or Edmonton, the western manufacturer has to include the cost of freight from Vancouver to Cobourg, and I consider that to be unfair.
I had a specific case where in actual fact, the freight involved was, I would say, something close to 50 per cent of the cost of the product. The product had to be delivered to Ontario, and then it was shipped back to Edmonton for stores there. This practice was changed, and the prices were quoted f.o.b. Edmonton from then on, but up to that time the department would receive the articles in Ontario and then pay the cost of freight back to Edmonton. The two centres which are probably most affected by this are Vancouver and Edmonton, which are the two major manufacturing centres west of Winnipeg. Finally, I suggest the department might well give consideration to strengthening their local offices in so far as local procurement is concerned, to the point where those local offices are able to advise on the procurement of major materials for the department.

In beginning the few remarks which I wish to make on the minister's estimates I should like to thank him, not only for the comprehensive and clear statement which he made this morning but also for his courtesy in sending two copies in
Supply-Defence Production advance over here so that we were able to follow him as he went along. We appreciate that very much. The statement was a revealing one. It revealed-though perhaps it was not required for that purpose because the purpose was obvious, once again that the key to defence production policy is defence policy. The key to the latter, as the minister pointed out in his statement, is the growing integration of our defence forces with those of the United States, which confirmed what the minister of defence made pretty clear in the debate on defence which we had the other day.
Defence production policy must obviously reflect that development in defence policy, which I admit has been going on for many years inevitably, perhaps inexorably, but a development which has gone farther now than ever before, as I ventured to say the other day, in our history. In the light of that, it is natural that defence production policy is now geared on the Canadian side, if I may put it this way, to United States defence policy or, if you would prefer to put it another way, to continental defence policy, which as it inevitably must be is under the major control of the United States, especially continental air defence policy. Of course, Mr. Chairman, this development, and the stage which it has now reached, is a far cry from the talk of emancipating our defence policy and defence production from the overpowering influence and control of the United States, the kind of talk we used to hear so often a few years ago.
The previous speakers from Port Arthur and Vancouver have urged on the minister that he or the government should lay down, as far as possible, a policy of direction in defence production so that procurement may be concentrated in those areas of underemployment, if you like, and surplus facilities. I have no particular argument to make to the minister in respect of my own area in that regard. As long as our defence relies to the extent it does now on nuclear deterrence, perhaps the most important defence production operation in the country is the production of uranium for the nuclear deterrent.
Having served in a government myself, I know of course, because this argument was used so often against us in earlier years, of the difficulties which exist in anything approaching a free economy in the direction by government of industrial and economic activity. Perhaps these is more opportunity, however, to do that in respect of an industrial activity which is so closely associated with government. In view of the minister's statement perhaps it will now be more closely associated than ever with government in peacetime, and probably there is
5674	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production more opportunity for this in defence production than any other form of industrial production. But while that may be the case, here again the integration, if I can use that word, of our defence and defence production activities with the United States will make it more difficult to direct those activities in Canada to areas where the government might wish to direct them.
The burden of the minister's statement this morning was on the importance of defence sharing with the United States as perhaps the only basis now on which we can maintain and develop a defence production industry in this country. I agree with him, in view of developments over the years, that that is probably the most important aspect of defence industry at the present time; but defence sharing must surely be more than getting orders from the United States for equipment for Canadian use. If it means anything, and if it really is a genuine reflection of the interdependence we talk so much about, it means sharing in Canada production for United States use, or certainly for joint use.
Our experience in this country in the last few years has not given us too much cause to believe that that kind of production sharing is going to develop as it should develop in joint or collective defence. Our experience, for instance, with the CF-105, the Arrow, has been a very unhappy one in that connection. If there ever was an opportunity for the United States to carry out in deed as well as in words recognition of the continental and collective concept of defence, it would have been to have shown at least a greater awareness of the desirability of using that Canadian airplane for general collective continental defence. We know what happened. Perhaps this is not the best example in the world to choose, because after the plane itself had been tested it must have been pretty difficult for the representatives of the Canadian government at that time to sell the idea of its use to the United States when the Canadian government itself was making up its mind that it was not going to be used in Canada. Indeed, in the words of the Prime Minister, it would be obsolete before it would come into squadron operation.
It would be hard enough even without that kind of qualification to persuade the United States to accept Canadian production for United States or for joint use, because it means we have to come up against all the pressures of United States industry. Perhaps they will be even greater than less in the days ahead. There is no place where those pressures are stronger, as I am sure my hon. friend knows better than I, than in the aircraft industry. As the defence industry in


the United States sees a reduction of orders, as it is seeing now, in some aspects of defence-I think of the Bomarc, for example, which is having its orders cut $900 million in the next five years-United States industry will be even more careful about permitting, if that is not too strong a word to use, its government to share with Canadian industry.
The minister's statement this morning seems to me to make perfectly clear that if we cannot somehow get Canadian industry into this kind of defence production sharing it will be awfully hard to maintain it, let alone develop it, in this country. I think the statement also makes clear, perhaps more by omission than in any other way, that at the present time the only real outlet for our defence industry outside Canada is the United States of America. Here the prospects, as I have just said, are at least uncertain. The minister points that out himself in his statement, and I would like to quote from the copy which he was good enough to let me have at the point where he says:
By actions such as these-
And he was talking about the steps which had been taken by the government.
-we have obtained a framework of United States policy and regulations which is favourable to Canadian participation.
Then he goes on:
But this is only the first step toward securing acceptance of Canadian sources.
Perhaps I do not need to suggest to the minister that the second step may be more difficult to take than the first. Perhaps he was not unduly pessimistic when he said earlier in this session, as reported on page 1269 of Hansard for February 23, 1959:
The real success of production sharing endeavours depends, to a large degree, upon the determination of Canadian industry vigorously to seek defence business in the United States either as prime or as subcontractors. In assuming this responsibility, Canadian industry must bear in mind that it will have to be competitive with United States industry in terms of technical competence, delivery and price.
That is quite true, of course, but it will have to be more than that. With all the support that the government can give it it will have to overcome the forces in Washington which will be very much on the alert to make sure, even if these obstacles can be overcome, that Canadian industry does not share to any extent in United States production which would constitute what they would call dangerous competition for their own producers.
So there are many difficulties ahead even though some of them perhaps have been overcome, and I am glad of course, as all hon. members of the house are, at the success which was achieved in eliminating those

aspects of the buy American law which remained. That was one step forward, but there are others, and I have mentioned some of the difficulties.
The minister also mentioned another one in his own statement, and that was the difficulty of tariff protection. On that point he has this to say:
I might explain that the exclusion of duty from a Canadian bid for evaluation purposes, under the waiver of the buy American policy, does not, in itself, provide for duty exemption when the material actually enters the United States, unless a dutyfree entry certificate has been granted.
I think it is accurate to say that the importance of this possible obstacle in the way of the development of our defence production through production sharing is shown by the fact that United States duties on defence equipment can be as high as 17 per cent, which would mean that Canadian industry, to get an order on business grounds alone, leaving out all these other things, would have to be 17 per cent more efficient.
The minister also mentioned the security difficulties, and he explained why he thought that most of these had been removed. I hope that is true, because I know what that could mean and, what is perhaps even more important, how it could be exploited by people in other countries. The minister said in his statement that it is the policy of the government to remove these difficulties. In his statement this morning, he said:
As I reported to the house last February 23, we set ourselves an immediate aim of increasing the participation of Canadian industry in the production and support of North American defence weapons; we also adopted a continuing objective which recognizes the long term nature of the problem with which we were faced, and looks to the co-ordination of the defence requirements, development, production and procurement of the two countries in order to achieve the best use of their respective production resources for their common defence.
That is, of course, the proper long range objective of Canadian policy in this important field, and unless that objective is shared by the United States-and we hope it will be shared-then the progress which the minister has mentioned as being desirable will not be achieved.
The minister mentioned this morning the steps which were being taken by the government to assist Canadian development, and a good deal of money is going to be spent on that. But as I followed his statement this morning, that assistance, and I am certainly not quarreling with him about it, wilj. be for Canadian development not so much for Canadian use as to get a share of United States orders.
Then the hon. gentleman said that one of the ways in which progress had been made
Supply-Defence Production was by getting the United States to recognize Canadian sources of supply. It seems to me that ever since the beginning of the second world war the United States has at least recognized Canadian sources of supply for defence equipment, but it is not this recognition that matters, as the minister himself indicated this morning in another part of his statement, so much as the use made by the United States of those sources of supply. He said that certain action had been taken for that purpose, and he thought certain progress had been made, and that in that action and in that progress the government had begun its contact with the United States authorities at the top-at the secretarial level in the United States and among the assistant secretaries responsible for the procurement programs of the three services. Then he went on to say that while it was necessary to begin at the top-and that is certainly true -nevertheless, any progress made at the top level will not be effective in terms of action unless it is followed up at lower levels, so I was glad to learn that the staff in Washington has been strengthened for this purpose.
It will also not be effective unless the same kind of impact can be made on congress as was made on the administration, and that is going to be more difficult. Not long ago I was reading reports of the hearings which took place in Washington on this subject of defence production, and in those hearings the secretary of defence showed an awareness of the joint role which must be played in the defence of the North American continent and of the importance of the United States recognizing the real necessity of cooperation in this matter, and he tried to explain this to the committee. But I read very shortly afterward that, perhaps alarmed by the reaction to his words in certain circles in the United States, he had attempted to remove what might have been a political risk by saying that certain people who had been concerned by his statement need not worry too much because, naturally, the position of the United States producer would always be considered as paramount. So there are going to be difficulties about carrying out this essential principle of defence sharing.
The minister said some time ago in the house in an earlier discussion, and I could quote from Hansard, that it is in the United States subcontract field that the greatest results can be achieved through the production sharing arrangements which the government had set up in conjunction with

Supply-Defence Production the United States. Today, he said with regard to that matter, and his words were, I think, very important:
I would emphasize that we are determined that any Canadian role in production sharing should include some of the more demanding work and not be limited to the pouring of concrete or to what is often called "metal bashing".
I agree with him that if the major portion of Canada's defence production in respect to this sharing arrangement takes the form of subcontracts or minor contracts we shall not get very far. It seems to me that it would oe intolerable, if Canadian producers wish to get this kind of defence business that they must accept the position of becoming marginal suppliers and subcontractors for United States industry, with all the instability and uncertainty that such a provision implies. How we could ever maintain and develop a defence production industry on any such basis as that I do not see, and I hope we will not have that experience. We could surely never expect the Canadian defence industry to expand or even, perhaps, to survive in conditions where it would become a mere adjunct of United States industry completely dependent on the generosity of United States producers and on the comprehension of the United States government.
That secondary position is certainly not acceptable. It would have the further great disadvantage of eliminating Canadian industry from major development work in this field, and I take it that the purpose of the expenditure which the minister talked about this morning to assist in Canadian development is not to develop Canadian industry so as to occupy such a subordinate continental role but to develop the Canadian defence industry on its own so that it could play its proper Canadian part.
As we all know, not very much scientific and technological research is done at the present time in Canada, at least in comparison with what is done across the line in the United States. We know that development work in air defence projects up to a year ago has partially filled and, I think on the whole, successfully filled this important gap. It was that development work which enabled Canadian industry to keep together large teams of scientific and highly qualified personnel working on defence technology.
According to the figures I received there were a year or so ago 7,100 scientific and engineering personnel in the aircraft industry or the associated electrical and electronic industries. If we in this country are eliminated from major development work in this field we will surely suffer a major blow because obviously we will gradually lose our

teams of qualified engineers and technicians and those who are at present teaching in Canadian institutions will not find the same employment opportunities in Canada in this field. That in its turn means we will become more and more dependent on United States technology not only for defence production but for our industrial development.
In this field of defence production there is a real danger that our industry will more and more give up development work for all practical purposes and even to a large extent the production of equipment and weapons, and our aircraft and allied industries, if they survive at all, will survive in a subsidiary role to far too great an extent as subcontractors for United States industry.
We have been told that if the western world is to survive we must accept interdependence. I think Canada in the past and at present is showing its willingness to work within that new system of relationships. We have participated very actively in all aspects of the NATO alliance through financial contributions and industrial contributions as well as through armed forces stationed in Europe. How can we go on doing this if the financial and other burdens involved in those commitments not only put us in a position where our territory itself has to be protected largely by the United States but where our own defence industries depend largely on the United States for their survival?
In the field of defence procurement and production we in this country in the past have accepted, and we must accept, the implications of interdependence with the United States and our other NATO allies, but if interdependence is to mean anything except as a word used in a speech, it has to be a two-way system of relationship. We in this country cannot be asked to make all the sacrifices in the name of interdependence. More specifically, I believe we cannot accept for the sake of an apparent interdependence the dislocation of our defence industries because of their too-close association with United States industry and because that association may lead to a dominant position over Canadian industry by those United States industries.
That is why I suggest that Canadian policy not only in the field of defence but in the field of defence production must be com-pletly re-appraised in consultation with our allies to see how our own interests can best be served and what can be our best contribution in a truly interdependent community.
Before I sit down I should like to mention three points which I feel should guide that kind of reassessment. First, I believe that free trade should be established as soon as possible between all NATO countries with

respect to defence production. Surely if we are going to recognize and be asked to implement interdependence effectively in this field we have to abolish tariff protection and all other obstacles to a free and easy movement of defence products within the North Atlantic alliance and certainly across the Canada-United States border. There is no difficulty in that respect in the other great defence area which is so much a threat to our security now that we have to spend these hundreds of millions of dollars, and if we are to be effective, economically and industrially, as we face this other great area, surely the time has come when we can remove these obstacles at least as they concern defence products.
When I say that I have a realization based on experience of the difficulties which will be advanced against a proposal of that kind and I know we have not made very much progress over the last ten years in the NATO alliance in removing these difficulties but I think we have to keep at it. After all, it is the test of the reality of our interdependence.
Second, I believe that sharing arrangements should not be restricted to the possible participation by one country in another nation's defence production program. At present I think that is Canada's position to far too great an extent. Perhaps the minister will be able to reassure me on that point by telling me how often and to what extent the United States has used Canadian production for its own purposes.
Defence sharing arrangements, as I understand them, must involve the assignment by the whole alliance of specific production sectors to individual countries so that those countries can really specialize in those fields and be sure to have sufficient details to develop manufacturing facilities under optimum conditions of efficiency without fear that other countries will enter into those production fields and dislocate existing facilities.
There again I know the problems involved. There is no better illustration than that found in the case of the CF-105. At the time that the CF-105 was first under consideration, I think I am fair in saying it was admitted in Washington that there was no plane in the United States that had been developed which was comparable to the CF-105 up to that time. I am talking about this plane two or three years ago. But that did not prevent the United States aircraft industry from going to work and developing planes which would be competitive with the CF-105 and
Supply-Defence Production which they eventually decided to use themselves. That is not the way to work out defence production sharing in the North Atlantic alliance.
Third, we should make sure that the specific programs assigned to a given country would be carried out effectively and that other countries could safely rely on the quality of the work being done by that country. We should do that by making arrangements to staff the development teams with the most qualified personnel available for this purpose in NATO, and to provide continuing information in consultation with all other interested countries in the alliance.
Almost ten years ago when those very principles which I have just mentioned were debated and discussed in the NATO council and in all the NATO agencies, they were agreed on in principle and there were defence production committees set up to see if they could be implemented in practice. I confess there was not very much progress made but that does not mean we should give up the search for that objective which is perhaps more important now than it was even in those days.
The three proposals I have outlined have, I know, far-reaching implications and results. This is the reason why they would be so difficult to achieve. Their achievement, however, would benefit all the countries inside the alliance and strengthen NATO which is so vital to the defence of the western world and provide a far better basis for the defence industry in Canada than that which we are likely to achieve if we have to depend almost entirely on the United States for the maintenance and development of that industry.
Surely it would be a wise thing for the Canadian government to take the initiative in this field and put forward proposals of this kind and pursue them at every possible opportunity, both in Paris at the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and-perhaps even more important-in Washington and in the Canadian-United States committees which have been set up in recent years.

speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Is the minister going to reply to the questions which have been asked?

Mr. Chairman, my first
remarks will be to reply to some of the suggestions made by the Leader of the Opposition. In my statement this morning I took great pains to make our position quite clear, as the Leader of the Opposition admitted, on this production sharing program that we have embarked on so extensively. I fully realize the difficulties we are going to meet and are meeting, but I also wish to be frank with the people and with the members
5678	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production of this committee. I say that we have obtained certain results. I am not overoptimistic because, as the Leader of the Opposition said, there is a powerful lobby in Washington and they have an aircraft industry of their own in the United States that needs to be sustained. On the other hand, since we have embarked on this program and really worked hard at it, we have obtained results and I am optimistic enough though to say that my hope is that in the months ahead, we shall have extensive orders and shall keep those good relations which exist at the present, not only with the superior officers in the defence department in Washington but also with all levels mentioned and officers down the line.
To come back to interdependence; as the Leader of the Opposition said, it is a two-way road. I want to make it perfectly clear, and I want to emphasize it here today, that on different occasions the Prime Minister has taken exactly the same position, and he did not pull his punches when he said that interdependence of the United States and Canada has to work both ways. This afternoon I want to make my position perfectly clear, as I have in the past, by saying that our strong and good neighbours to the south have to come across to the Canadian people in this production sharing. That is what I am out to achieve and that is what my department is working for. When I present my estimates another year I hope to be able to report that I have obtained some results.
The Leader of the Opposition talked about some figures. I have a list of contracts in front of me which amounts to $31 million of prime contracts and the $20 million that I mentioned this morning in my statement. 1 tell the Leader of the Opposition that it is practically all for the United States army. This is an example: Radome panels, $19,000; calibration and repair of test equipment, $391,000; components for communication systems, $3,568,000; engine spares for the United States, $2,873,000; equipment and spare parts for radomes, $252,000; engine spares, again for the United States, $4,197,000; electronic spares, $443,000; and so on.
I have here a long list of subcontracts also which are in great part for the armed forces of the United States. I appreciate very much the kind remarks of the Leader of the Opposition about the statement I made this morning and about my sending him a copy, which was a pleasure. I also extend to him my appreciation of the remarks he made this afternoon. I have taken note of them and I shall be pleased to peruse and study them in Hansard.
I should just like to answer my good friend from Lapointe who spoke extensively this


morning with a lot of charity because we know each other pretty well. He spoke about the dictatorial powers given to the Minister of Defence Production by certain sections of the Defence Production Act. In reply I wish to state that by statute sections 23 to 31, inclusive, terminate on July 31 of this year, and the government is not renewing these sections which give dictatorial powers to the Minister of Defence Production. Therefore, I hope that my hon. friend from Lapointe will not be worried over the fact that I shall be a dictator by desire.
He also mentioned that there was a substantial increase in the budget. I explained in my statement this morning that the increase in the budget is primarily due to this $5 million increase for the new program of technological work that we intend to do and to continue with this production sharing, where we have an amount of $7 million in different items to help Canadian contractors compete in the United States field.
The hon. member for Port Arthur expressed his interest in the Canadian Car and Foundry plant at Fort William, but some of its employees are from Port Arthur. As the hon. member knows, a delegation came here to meet us on two different occasions to try to have work placed in this plant. To the delegation consisting of all the social clubs and the authorities of these two cities we expressed our sincere hope that we could do something for this area. To be perfectly frank, I want to tell the people what the Canadian Car and Foundry Company are doing at the present time. I want this to go on record. The main activity of the Canadian Car and Foundry Company Limited, Fort William, has been the fabrication of centre sections, wings, and surface controls for the CS2F on a subcontract basis from de Havil-land. In addition, they are fabricating Otter wings, also on a subcontract basis for de Havilland. At present, Canadian Car and Foundry have approximately 10 CS2F components to complete at an approximate value of $1,211,478. Canadian Car and Foundry are working on 25 sets of Otter wings at an approximate value of $250,000. They also have some small contracts for Harvard components.
The Fort William facility has also been actively soliciting business in the United States under production sharing arrangements but as of the present time they have not yet been successful in obtaining any contracts. The development of the Bobcat vehicle, to which the hon. member referred, is continuing very well at the Montreal facilities of this company but it will be some months before any decision can be made about its production. I have said, and I have expressed the same view to the personnel of

my department, that in this production sharing we hope to have the chance to bring some production work into the plant at Fort William.
In reply to the hon. member for Vancouver South who spoke of spreading defence contracts across the country and especially encouraging the west coast,-and I should like this reply to apply to the hon. member for Port Arthur as well-we are striving as much as possible in our purchasing in the different spheres of this department to purchase in the areas affected. For the information of the members of the committee I may say I have received very strong reproaches at different times from hon. members who have said that they used to sell to defence production in certain areas and today they are losing the chance to make those sales. Well, this is because we are trying to buy in areas where the articles are needed and where the food is needed across the country. This is why in the maritimes, for example, this year, although our purchases across the country were down 6 per cent, we had an increase of 20 per cent. We have tried to purchase more in the areas affected, the maritimes, Quebec, Ontario, the three prairie provinces and the Pacific coast. The Pacific coast is an area where there are certain problems. Of course we have to think cost-wise and we have to think of quality but I can assure the committee that as much as possible we strive to do our utmost to buy locally in the areas I have just mentioned.
In my statement I tried to give hon. members a clear picture of what we are doing in defence production and our hopes of improving Canadian industry by production sharing. But I want to admit very frankly that I know the troubles and the work that lie ahead for the officials we have appointed in the United States, the officials of the department here and the government itself in getting substantial orders from United States industry. I want to emphasize that I wish it to be clearly understood by the United States authorities that if we enter into production sharing for the defence of the North American continent it is a two-way road and that there has to be a give and take attitude. That is my position and, as I said a while ago, I hope we will get results in the months ahead.

I should like the minister to clarify one point in the remarks he has just made. It has to do with the distribution of contracts within the country. Does he not realize that at a time when the total value of contracts awarded throughout the country is declining and the number of those in the armed forces is not materially decreasing the percentage spent on food 66968-9-360
Supply-Defence Production supplies and the like for the forces, involving mostly local expenditures, would be a relatively larger proportion, and that when he gives statistics, as he did a moment ago, for the increase in purchases in the maritimes they can be quite misleading on this somewhat difficult subject, although I am not questioning their accuracy? Does he have that in mind and does he not also realize that the completion of camp Gage-town and the movement of more troops into that camp would have some bearing on the quantity of local purchases in the area? I want to make that observation because I think that if the statement of the minister on the point is left as he made it it is capable of creating a wrong impression. While the statistics are accurate enough, the statement is not quite adequate in doing justice to the subject.

In reply to the hon. member for Ottawa West, he will realize that the maritime provinces have an economic council which is very active in encouraging industry and selling merchandise in the martimes. The figures I just gave were given offhand but we found that a lot of the purchases for the maritimes were made through the city of Montreal. For the last year we have been concentrating more buying in the maritimes. For example, potatoes used to be purchased in Montreal. They were produced in the maritimes, shipped to Montreal and then sent back to the maritimes. That is just one example of better results by following the policy of buying locally. I gave a figure indicating an increase of 20 per cent over the amount bought in the maritimes the previous year, but if the quantity was very small the previous year it has to be increased by one-fifth to get the increase of 20 per cent for the year I am talking about.

I wish the minister well in his effort to increase purchases in that area but the point I want to make is that the statistics by themselves are capable of being very misleading. I have been fairly familiar with them in the past. If he will look at some of the places where purchases are indicated as having been made he will find, for instance, that meat purchases from the Burns Company used to be listed as having taken place in Ottawa, which was completely misleading. Perhaps I do not need to pursue the subject beyond indicating that I hope he is making some progress and I trust he will not assume that statistics such as he has given are proof of his success in that field.
