There is another point I want to raise having to do with a matter that arose during the discussion of the Department of National Defence estimates the other day. We were dealing with item No. 222 which is listed as being for the construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and major equipment for the Royal Canadian Air Force. When we look at the particulars of that item as found on page 314 we see one major item under major procurement of equipment namely aircraft and engines.
When I asked questions about that item I discovered from the Minister of National Defence that there was included in that procurement item an expenditure of $45 million for the termination of the Arrow contract. The point I wish to raise is this. I had assumed that the termination of contracts was something that was still treated under a separate item as was the case during the last war and subsequent thereto and that the item to which I have referred provided the Department of National Defence with the authorization and the money to procure equipment and supplies and to take care of military pay and civil staff salaries. I had thought that these other items for termination of contracts were items that came properly under the Department of Defence Production as they did in earlier years and under predecessor departments.
Since I understand that the termination of this contract is being carried out under the minister's jurisdiction, I want to pursue this point. How does the minister derive authority from the wording of item No. 222 which I have just quoted, for the expenditure of this very large sum of money on the termination of a contract with respect to which equipment is not being procured this year but whose purpose is to carry out the liquidation and termination of a Contract which was concluded in the last fiscal year? For the life of me I cannot find anything in the language used in that estimate that would warrant the expenditure of moneys for the purpose of terminating a contract. It seems to me that there is no authority whatever to spend this $45 million under that item. I have no doubt that the treasury officials have looked at this point and that there is some answer. Whatever the answer is I should like to have it, and if there is no answer I should like to have the matter corrected because it seems to me that in this way the house is not being given information to which it is entitled.
So that the minister will have some references to the practice on this subject, if he will look at the estimates for the year ending March 31, 1953, item 81, page 11, he will find


there an item in the estimates of the Department of Defence Production to provide for the liquidation of contracts and so on. He will find the same thing in the estimates of a year earlier, and so on back through the years. The last year for which there was any estimate comparable to this $45 million for the termination of a contract is in the year ending March 31, 1948. He will find an item No. 569 in the estimates of that year for his predecessor department, reconstruction and supply.
I could go back through the years, but in that year the item was $2.5 million and the previous year the item had been $36 million. Now, this year the expenditure for such an item is $45 million for this one contract alone, yet we have no special item for it at all. Unless there is some adequate explanation, I think the matter should be rectified. I wonder if the minister could give an explanation?

In reply to the hon. member for Ottawa West I would say I am advised by my officials that the Department of Defence Production, since its inception in 1951, has never had a separate vote for the termination of contracts. These costs are created by the Department of National Defence and cannot be separated from production costs. We are really acting for the Department of National Defence. The items referred to by the hon. member for Ottawa West related to the termination of disputed world war II contracts, and that is why they were the subject of a separate vote. Since the inception of the Department of Defence Production in 1951 there has never been a separate vote for cancellation charges under a current contract. Does that satisfy the hon. member?

It is not quite as full an explanation as I would wish, but I thank the minister for it. There have never been termination problems in connection with contracts of this size or scope since world war II; that is quite elementary.
The point here is that that item and the amount to be paid for the termination of those contracts, some of which were disputed, was always provided through the Department of Defence Production and its predecessor department and passed upon by this committee. The point I wish to raise now has two facets. The first question I have sought to raise is as to the explanation of what appears to be a misapplication of funds voted for procurement of specific equipment, and not being used for that at all but being used for the settlement of claims arising out of the termination of a contract. This is the No. 1 point with which the minister has dealt.

The other point I want to raise is as to the policy of the government in not providing a separate item to come before the committee because it seems to me to be quite misleading to have an item in one year which provides several hundreds of millions of dollars for procurement of a particular type of aircraft and then find, in the next year, when you go to compare the figures, there is nothing in the printed record anywhere to indicate any lesser amount being spent. However, when we start asking questions about it we find the item is not to procure that kind of equipment at all but is to settle termination charges of a contract.
I think the minister will follow my point there. There is no way by which one doing research on the estimates produced to the house can find that the figure is not as it appears at all, and this must be found out by questions. It seems to me this is a practice which should be looked at for future action because while it may be true that, in a large procurement item, there may be small incidental items in connection with termination of contracts they are only a tiny percentage of the total. However, here we have $45 million out of $146 million being spent on termination charges, yet all of it being shown as if the whole $146 million were being spent for procurement This is likely to be misleading to hon. members, and I am sure that is not what the minister wants to do at all. I would ask him to look at this again to see that if the question ever arises in the future, and I hope it will not, the item will be shown in different form and one that will be clear to all hon. members.

I wish to thank the hon. member for Ottawa West for asking these questions, and I can assure him we will study his remarks very attentively. My officials tell me there was a major cancellation in 1954, which was taken out of the national defence budget and there was no vote in defence production. I feel this is a very good point, and I shall be glad to look at it and give the information to the hon. member.
What is the authority for spending the money in that way? I cannot, for the fife of me, follow that.
I should like to tell the hon. member that we do not spend the money; we are the agents for national defence.

What is the authority for it? You have to handle the mechanics of spending it, and you do not spend money without proper legal authority-at least, the department did not use to do so. It seems to me there is no authority granted for spending the money for that purpose.
66968-9-360J
Supply-Defence Production

I think, by the charter of defence production, when we get orders from national defence for a certain work, it is a question for national defence and the Department of Finance. We execute the orders when we receive them, and it is those two departments that are interested in this problem. I think there is a good point there, and it should be looked into, as the hon. member suggests.

There is just one other thing. I take it the item would not permit such expenditures as keeping a small number of these men at work, as was suggested at the time of the Arrow cancellation. These funds were for procurement or legal termination of the contract, but the language would not be wide enough for that, would it?

I am afraid I have not the answer to that question with me this afternoon. I admit we are handling the termination charges under this vote. However, so far as changing from procurement to cancellation is concerned, I am afraid I have not got the information available just now.

Mr. Chairman, it has been suggested that the money which was available for termination of the contract could have been used by the company to keep the employees at work for a time until they got other work. The question my hon. friend is asking is whether this money could have been used under the vote for that purpose.

As far as defence production is concerned, I think the Leader of the Opposition will agree with me that it was the government's decision to terminate. We are executing the orders we receive from national defence, and that is as far as our department concerns itself. As long as the work is paid for by national defence, through us if you will, it is not for defence production to find out under what vote this money is provided.

There is a second point there, Mr. Chairman. Once the contract is cancelled, I take it the defence production department would not pay for keeping the men at work after termination? There would be no authority for that. Surely the accounts of the company are audited and checked?

In the cancellation charges it must be admitted that we have paid a substantial amount to the men for their vacation pay, their severance pay and so on. We have paid all these amounts out of that and have completely complied with the full labour contracts and paid out everything that the labour contracts demanded. It comes back to the same question, that it was an

Supply-Defence Production order from national defence and we are executing the order we received from national defence.

But my point is that in executing the order received from national defence you paid only those charges you were obligated to pay under the contract. You paid the labour charges, for example, that you were obligated to pay under that contract, and you did not or could not go beyond that and give money to the company merely to pay men in addition to what was provided under the labour and other contracts?

Certainly not, Mr. Chairman. We consented absolutely to paying all charges that were demanded by the labour contract for all the employees. That we accepted; but we could not keep on paying afterwards the men sitting around the plant not doing anything, and we were not justified in making any other payments.
So it is now clear, Mr. Chairman, that this money could not have been used by the company to keep people at work after the contract had been terminated.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I would like to congratulate the minister for the progress he has made in negotiations with the United States, particularly with respect to the buy American act and the long list of items which he and his officials have negotiated and made exempt from the buy American act, and also the progress they have made with respect to tariff waivers. I think the minister has an excellent staff who have done an outstanding job of negotiating these concessions with the United States. As a matter of fact, I think the minister has staff which he could not excel if he had taken a long time in putting them together. The minister told us quite frankly, Mr. Chairman, that he has problems. We feel that these problems are not particularly of his making, but that most of them are grief caused by other departments of government and the Minister of Defence Production and his staff have to make the best of such bad jobs as are passed to them.
For example, the minister told us this morning that the progress made in the first six months of this year had demonstrated approximately $32 million in prime contracts for military equipment for branches of the United States armed forces. This sounds like a significant achievement and undoubtedly it represents a great deal of hard work and laborious effort on the part of the minister and his staff. Yet it seems he has been fighting a rearguard action, because I have here a press clipping from the Toronto Star of July 6, 1959,


entitled "Aircraft Parts Exports Show Sharp Decline" and it is based on a Canadian Press dispatch from Ottawa which says:
Canada's domestic exports in May fell $51,500,000 from the same month last year due mainly to a sharp reduction in sales of aircraft and parts, the bureau of statistics said.
In other words, the reduction in export of aircraft and parts in the first six months of this year was more substantial than the total number of small prime contracts obtained for Canadian producers to produce military equipment for various branches of the United States government. This indicates the magnitude of the problem which we face. The minister, as I have said, is fighting a rearguard action, and this has been the case ever since the cancellation of the Avro Arrow, when we lost our great leverage with the United States. We have to be realistic in our dealings with them.
Certainly they want to co-operate with us, and certainly the high level official talks taking place between the minister and his staff and their opposite numbers in Washington are productive. There is the greatest amount of co-operation and a real desire on the part of our United States friends to try to work out satisfactory solutions. But they have to operate within the context of the political situation existing in the United States of America, and they have problems in putting into effect their good intentions. We are just babes in the wood if we do not realize that if business is bad in the United States of America the pressure of the aircraft and other defence industries down there on their government is going to be very great indeed. If business is good in the United States and they have full employment, then probably it would not be too difficult to get a few prime contracts for Canadian producers. But in times when business is not good in the United States and there is a great deal of unemployment in various parts of the country, it is unrealistic for us to think that we are going to go down there and negotiate large prime contracts for Canadian producers unless we use the leverage we have in negotiation with them.
We have a number of things we can use as leverage. We have a number of geographical requirements which they have to ask for from time to time, and there are a number of concessions which the United States asks us for, and we do have some bargaining power. It is very difficult within the context of the political situation within the United States of America, without using such leverage as we have available to us, to negotiate any sizable prime contracts, and particularly defence production contracts.

Mr. Chairman, with those introductory remarks I would like to ask the minister a few questions. I would like to commence with reference to the Avro Arrow CF-105 and continue a question asked by the hon. member for Ottawa West and the Leader of the Opposition. I would like to ask the minister if any study was made of the cost of continuing to completion the 37 aircraft which were under construction at the time the cancellation order was issued?
At the request of the hon. member for Trinity I am asking for the file of the study made of the CF-105 to be brought down. If he will continue I will get that information.
I have a further question, Mr. Chairman. Of the completed five aircraft, Nos. 1 to 5, were they turned over to Crown Assets Disposal Corporation for disposal?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

And are they still in the
custody of the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation?

They are being dismantled at the present time and arrangements are being made with the United States government for the return of the engines and the fireheads and the classified materials which are in these planes. They will be dismantled.
Upon what terms and conditions were the planes offered for sale by the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation?

The fact is that the ministry of national defence gave orders to my department, and my department to crown assets that all equipment should be taken out of these aircraft and that they should be reduced to scrap. Those were the orders received from national defence.
Did the Minister of National Defence turn them over to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation as surplus equipment? Did he declare them surplus?
They were declared surplus, yes, and the instruction was given that all equipment should be taken out of the aircraft and they should be reduced to scrap.
What was the statutory authority by which the Minister of National Defence determined the method of disposal by the crown assets corporation?

This was an aircraft constructed not only by Canadian engineers and the Canadian air force but also by the United States. It was classified. It could not have been sold on an open market. I do not see any other solution available to the Minister
Supply-Defence Production of National Defence but to turn it to scrap. That is the way the situation was.

That does not answer my
question. I assume there could not have been very much classified material about the plane, because we were told in this house it was obsolescent and that it would not have been useful by the time it was put into squadron service. If the minister of defence had declared it surplus it could perhaps have been sold by the crown assets corporation in the normal way, and I am wondering what statutory authority the Minister of National Defence has for deciding it should be disposed of in some other manner.

After the contract had been cancelled, any classified material was taken out, and I think the only solution was to have these aircraft reduced to scrap. I wish to say to the hon. member for Trinity that to my knowledge-and I can be corrected by the Minister of National Defence if I am not right-the department tried on different occasions to make a research bid of this plane in the United Kingdom, without success. Terms were not discussed, and they were not interested in the least. So I am still of the opinion that there was no alternative but to take out all the equipment from these planes and then have them disposed of in the only way possible.
What parts of the plane were classified?

One would practically have to go over the whole plane-hydraulics, fire control, engine, electronic equipment. With the experience which the hon. member has with regard to planes he will certainly know that there are hundreds of parts in that plane which were classified. I am certainly not versed enough to give him a complete list of the classified materials in the CF-105 this afternoon.

It must have been a good aircraft if there were hundreds of classified parts in it.
There was a request that plane No. 6 and subsequent aircraft be photographed in the factory during the process of destruction, and the minister, in answer to a question in the House of Commons, said the reason photographs were not allowed was because classified fire control apparatus had been installed in the planes. Is that correct?
That is correct.
Can the minister tell us on how many of these planes fire control apparatus had been installed?

There is perhaps a difference of opinion there. The fire control system for
5684	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production several of the planes was in manufacture; I cannot say definitely if it was installed in some of the planes, but it was definitely there in the plant with other classified material when the cancellation started. It was not only on my part that I took the decision, but I had the concurrence of the Avro people not to have photographs taken at that time in the plant.

The reply the minister gave to the house earlier was that it was because of the Hughes fire control system that photographers were not allowed to be present at the time of the destruction. However, it is my understanding that there was no fire control installed on aircraft No. 6 and subsequent aircraft. Can the minister advise the committee whether or not that information is correct?
I am told that the fire control system was not installed in these planes.
Was, or was not?
Was not.
A final question on the subject. Does the minister not think that this very important chapter in Canadian history should have been recorded and filmed for posterity?

I do not think it was a very important chapter in the pages of Canadian history-in the pages of aviation history-to see the work of years being scrapped. I do not think it would have been of advantage to Canada.

I cannot let that comment ride without replying that I think it was an important chapter in Canadian history. I think it represented the greatest single achievement in Canadian aviation history, and the greatest combined effort of design and development ever undertaken in this country. Not only that, I regret, and I want to put this on record again, that this government did not have the courage to finish No. 6 and let it take the world's speed record away from the Lockheed 104. I think this is a matter which will cause regret to Canadians for decades to come-that when we had reached a stage where, in a few weeks of additional development and testing, this plane could have captured the world's speed record for this country, the decision should have been made not only to stop work on the plane but to cut up the corpse and put it underground as soon as possible.

I wonder if I can ask a question about the cancellation of this contract? Hon. members will, no doubt, recall that the Prime Minister had some very severe things to say about the Avro company because


they discharged their staff as soon as they received an order from the minister's department to do so.
Mr. Richard Jackson in the Sudbury Star of June 20 had this to say:
What evidence have the members of parliament of there being something less than the loyalty of political impartiality normally expected of a civil service?
That shocking telegram that ordered the immediate firing "at once" of the 14,000 Avro workers was sent by some bureaucratic brass hat in defence production.
Would the minister say whether this telegram was sent without his concurrence or with his concurrence.

We sent the telegram to cancel all work on the Arrow and the Iroquois engine. This telegram was sent with my concurrence. I will admit frankly I was under the impression that the idea of sending the telegram at that time was to prevent further buying of expensive material for the plane or for the engine, but that the men would continue for their ordinary period of time on notice, which was two weeks or three weeks. I was most surprised myself to hear the same evening the men were let out that afternoon. The telegram was sent with my concurrence.
Could the minister read the telegram for the committee now?
Mr. Chairman, I have not got it with me; the telegram has been tabled and is on Hansard.
I think it might be convenient to have it in Hansard at this point.
Oh, oh.
This is a very serious charge made by a responsible journalist against the honesty and integrity of senior civil servants of this country.
Read it yourself.

If the hon. gentleman is finished mumbling perhaps I could be allowed to continue. The minister has said this telegram was sent with his concurrence. I accept his word at once. I am sure it was. However, in order to remove all doubt about this serious and shocking reflection I believe the whole story should appear all together in one place.
It will be recalled, of course, that my friend the hon. member for Laurier had the telegram put on the record after the Prime Minister said he expected the company to go on employing these people on work that was not going to be accepted and for which the company could not be paid-a very odd attitude it seemed to me for the Prime Minister

to take-but there is no doubt whatever that the telegram did say specifically that the work was to cease immediately. I believe that the record should be straight.
Does the hon. member want to put on the record again a copy of the telegram? I do not have a copy in my files today.
Would the minister get it and put it in the record a little later on?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it correct that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate would like the minister to read into the record a document that has already been tabled?
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but I did not hear you.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is demanding that the minister put into the record something that has already been put into it?

I would not like to use the word "demand". I am not making a demand. I was asking the minister if he would be good enough to do it so that the record of this transaction would be complete in one place. The reason I am asking that is because, although it is on the record, it does not seem to be easy to find. My friend the hon. member for Ottawa West appears to have it and perhaps he could read it.
Just say "yes".

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: For the sake of good order, it is generally admitted by all that this telegram has actually been tabled and is in the records of the house. It would be a repetitious occurrence if we continued the debate concerning the tabling of a document that has already been tabled. I appreciate the hon. member's explanation that he is not demanding that it be tabled because it would be out of order for him to demand that the minister table a document. It is the opinion of the Chair that since this telegram is already on the record and should be quite easily located it is really repetitious to request that we continue the debate regarding the matter.

I still think we are entitled to debate this item under the administration of the Department of Defence Production and ask all the questions we wish about the termination of the contract and other related matters.
It is out of order.
I know that my friend the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I must point out to the hon. member for Ottawa West that the
Supply-Defence Production Chair has not indicated that hon. members of the opposition would be prevented from asking questions they wish to ask. I am simply referring to the unnecessary tabling of a document which has already been tabled. This has nothing to do with questions that might be put by hon. members of the opposition.

I wish to say something about the telegrams. The reason they were not presented to the house when the Prime Minister spoke as recorded at page 1306 of Hansard is quite obvious. He made certain statements there about the ceasing of the work and the fact that the A. V. Roe company should not have let their employees go immediately. After considerable hounding and questioning of the government the opposition was able to have the telegrams presented to the house. They are printed in an appendix to Hansard of February 27, 1959, at page 1487.
By agreement.

When they were tabled and printed in Hansard it became immediately obvious that the Prime Minister's whole point on this aspect of the subject had been completely wrong. If hon. members will check the page references I have given they will see that the telegram to the A. V. Roe company, marked attention Mr. J. L. Plant, Malton, TCO via CN telegraph from Mr. D. L. Thompson, of the Department of Defence Production, Ottawa, contains in it a direct instruction in this language, "You shall cease all work immediately." Then the corresponding telegram sent about 12.30 p.m. on the same Friday was directed to Orenda Engine, attention Mr. E. K. Brownridge, from Mr. D. L. Thompson of the Department of Defence Production. It used precisely the same language, "You shall cease all work immediately." The minister has today admitted that he approved of those telegrams.
I never denied it.
The minister is quite right.
Precisely.
More innuendo.
You are leaving the impression that he did deny it which is wrong.

I never suggested that the minister denied it. Indeed, I never discussed his relationship up to this moment. I was just coming to it. I was saying and I will repeat again that the minister now admits these telegrams were sent with his concurrence and knowledge. His position is quite clear on that. It become abundantly clear from the contents of the telegrams and from what
5686	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production the minister said earlier in answer to the discussion we had a few moments ago about the items he could allow by way of salary to the employees of the A. V. Roe company,- allowance for severance pay, holiday pay, and so on-that he allowed those under agreements that were outstanding with the men. That was quite proper and I have no criticism of that. It becomes clear that the statement made to the house by the Prime Minister on February 23, four days before the telegrams were presented to us but three days after the contracts were terminated, that the Prime Minister's remarks as they appear at the bottom of the first column of page 1306 are not in accordance with what was done or in accordance with what could be done under the contracts. That is where the situation stands now. It is a good thing that this matter has at long last been cleared up so that everyone interested in this subject can know exactly where the responsibility for the immediate dismissal of these men lay, why it was done and what allowance has been made in respect of it.

Yes; it seems to me it is now perfectly clear that the Prime Minister did not know what he was talking about when he said this termination of contract money could have been used to keep people at work in the A. V. Roe Company after that telegram had been sent. It seems to me that the journalist in question did not know what he was writing about when he made the reflection on the integrity of senior officials of the department for sending the telegram which we know was sent with the knowledge and under the authority of the minister.

Do I understand from the minister that the taking of a picture of the CF-105 before it was destroyed was not allowed? If this is so, how is it that the Postmaster General got a picture of it and was so proud of it that he put it on a stamp? I would like to get an explanation because he said that this event was not so important after all. There seems to be a difference of opinion or a misunderstanding between the Postmaster General and the Minister of Defence Production.
In reply to the hon. member for St. Denis, I wish to tell him that the CF-105 has been filmed and photographed. They are all over the country and he can get many copies of pictures of the CF-105.
Will the stamp be declared surplus?
If the hon. member has any money left over he can buy the stamps and put the surplus stamps in his pocket.
Can the minister tell us whether the five completed Arrows were ever offered to the royal aeronautical establishment in Great Britain for testing purposes?

Mr. Chairman, the CF-105's
were offered to the aeronautical research establishment in the United Kingdom and they were turned down.
What were the terms and conditions of the offer?
They were offered; there were no terms or conditions. They were offered and they were turned down. No terms were discussed.
Were they offered free?
I cannot say they were offered free. No terms were discussed. They were not interested; they did not want them.

Mr. Chairman, there seems to be an awful lot of confusion and buck-passing between the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production on this whole matter of the disposal of these things. I have asked the Minister of National Defence in the house who was responsible for the disposal of the aircraft, and he said it was a matter for defence production. Today the Minister of Defence Production says it was done under orders from the Minister of National Defence; similarly, with the Iroquois engine. I submit that these two ministers should get together in the future and agree on responsibility.

I have gone over the statements and the questions put by the hon. member for Eglinton when he was sitting on this side of the house. I have gone over the debates for 1953, 1954 and 1955. Since he is not in his seat today, I am sure the Minister of Defence Production will be very glad to answer a question in which his colleague is most interested. What is the breakdown of our purchases in the United States with regard to defence procurement compared with those in the United Kingdom?

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate remarked the other day, this is the black book. Mutual defence procurement between Canada and the United States is carried on under the joint statement of principles for economic cooperation which was signed by the two countries in 1950. When the present defence program was initiated, it was necessary to place fairly substantial contracts in the United States for equipment urgently required and not at the time produced in Canada. With respect to the Canadian defence contracts placed in the United States, the figure for 1958-59 is $23.1 million to our credit. The

net value of Canadian defence contracts placed in the United Kingdom was $10,590,000. We have a credit with the United States because we cancelled more than we placed. We got a credit of $23.1 million, and we placed orders to the amount of $10,590,000 with the United Kingdom.
Can the minister tell us whether in the $32 million prime contracts which he mentioned in his statement this morning were included the turbines being installed at Grand Bend?
No, Mr. Chairman.

I have another question for the minister. I am sure this will be a pleasant recollection for him and I am sure it will be of great interest to my hon. friend from Montmagny-L'Islet. Sometime during last fall the minister paid a visit to an establishment called La Fonderie de l'lslet in the county of Montmagny-L'Islet, and we read in the paper a few days later that he paid a visit to these people in the hope that he could offer them some work from his department. Since his talk with the officials of the company, I wonder whether anything has materialized in concrete form?
Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member for Lapointe has got things twisted up a little bit. They really invited me to see the facilities of their plant.
Is any production going on at the present time in this country of F-86's or CF-lOO's?
Just the production of spares, Mr. Chairman.

In view of the fact that the CF-100 will be in use for some years, presumably, and the F-86 will not be replaced by the F-104 completely until 1963, according to the minister's own figures this morning, how are those squadrons to be maintained at strength if only spares are being produced?

The spares are to maintain the aircraft. The Leader of the Opposition will admit with me that, as far as defence production is concerned, all I can do is act when I get an order from the Minister of National Defence. I am just the agent to purchase; I have no more authority than that.

Perhaps this is irregular, but I wonder whether I could ask the Minister of National Defence what happens when a CF-100 or the F-86 crashes and he asks the Minister of Defence Production for a replacement for that plane and the minister says, "we are not making any more"?

We have a reserve of CF-lOO's which are capable of replacing any of those which happen to crash.
66968-9-361
Supply-Defence Production
Then, it is considered that there is a sufficient reserve of F-86's and CF-lOO's to maintain those squadrons at full strength until some years from now when they will be replaced by other planes?
That is correct, utilizing spares to replace any spare parts which may be destroyed, where practicable.

I have another question for the minister. I must apologize if I implied in my question that he visited the plant in Montmagny-L'Islet on his own initiative, and I quite accept his correction. I wonder whether after his visit he has been able to give some word to La Fonderie de L'lslet either by way of tender or by negotiation?

Mr. Chairman, I recollect that they tendered on some contract but as far as I can remember they have received no contracts from the government. I know they tendered several times on different contracts.
Is the minister aware that they had a contract from the government and that that contract has been cancelled? Not only did they get no contract but the one they had was cancelled.
How many years ago?
I mean lately.
Well, it is pretty hard to cancel a contract if you do not have any.
They had a contract to make some postal boxes for the Post Office Department and now they are out of work.
If the hon. member for St. Denis wants to get information about postal boxes he will have to ask the Postmaster General.
I wonder whether it would be imposing too much on the minister to ask him to give us a breakdown of defence procurement for the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
The net value of head office contracts placed with firms in Quebec in 1958-59 was $218,408,000, and in Ontario $264,040,000.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister whether the construction work for the air force at Foymount in the county of Renfrew is under his jurisdiction?
It is under a crown company, defence construction.

May I ask the minister these questions? I do not expect that he can answer them at the moment but I hope he

Supply-Defence Production will. Were tenders called for all federal government contracts in connection with the expansion of the Foymount air station? If so, can the minister give us the names and head office addresses of the firms to whom these contracts were awarded, together with the names and addresses of unsuccessful bidders for these contracts? Lastly, were the contracts awarded to the lowest tenderer in each case? I should like to have that information very much.

The contracts were all
awarded on the basis of tenders and generally were awarded to the lowest tenderers, but it is practically impossible for me to give the names of the tenderers and the amounts this afternoon. If the hon. member would like to have the information I would be pleased to procure it for him. I am sorry I have not got it with me this afternoon.
I did not expect the minister would have the information this afternoon but I thought I would ask him these questions so that possibly we could have the information tomorrow.
I will be pleased to get that information for the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, at this stage of his estimates I wonder whether the minister would care to comment briefly on the report and recommendations of the estimates committee of last year under the general headings of destroyer escort program, performance bonds, general comments and recommendations and, in particular, general conclusion of the report, No. 5.

No. 1 is the destroyer escort program. The observations and recommendations of the standing committee on estimates with respect to the destroyer escort program were dealt with in considerable detail when the estimates of my department were last presented-Hansard, August 9, 1958, pages 3238 to 3240. At this time, however, I should like to say that in the very near future tenders will be invited covering the construction of a naval fleet supply tanker. We are going to call for tenders for the naval fleet supply tanker.
No. 2 is performance bonds. Last year I reported that considerable thought had been given to the questions of accepting performance bonds and/or pay-and-performance bonds. Since that time the cabinet has agreed that for a trial period commencing January 1, 1959 contractors should be given the option of submitting either surety bonds or security deposits to ensure due performance of work on government contracts. Treasury board has approved three types of surety bonds which are to be regarded as the standard, acceptable


bonds for government contracts, namely a bid bond, a performance bond, and a labour and material payment bond.
With regard to the question of improving liaison between my department and the Department of National Defence, I should like to point out that while there has been very close liaison in the past between the two departments there is now an even closer liaison. The procedures which have been established to carry out our production sharing program with the United States involve a senior policy committee comprised of senior officials of not only the departments of defence production and national defence but also external affairs, finance and the United States department of defence, a steering group to handle the co-ordination of all activities and a number of working groups consisting of technical personnel to work out the detailed arrangements on specific projects of mutual interest. The officials of the departments of defence production and national defence are intimately associated in all these activities.
I am also very pleased that the Minister of National Defence has appointed the deputy minister of defence production as a member of the defence research board. The other specific recommendations, and my comments on them, are as follows:
That the department encourage, assist and coordinate the growth of technical skills and knowledge in the Canadian industry as a program of industrial preparedness.
As members may be aware, the Defence Production Act requires the minister to organize, mobilize and conserve Canadian industrial resources to meet the current and prospective needs of defence. I would assure the house that I am anxious to discharge fully this statutory obligation, with which this recommendation of the committee is in keeping.
For the benefit of those who are unfamiliar with the department's operations, particularly those who were not members of the standing committee, I might explain briefly some of the ways in which we attempt to accomplish this task. First, in purchasing the supplies requisitioned by the armed services we recognize the services cannot always depend in an emergency on the production resources of other countries or the maintenance of normal ocean shipping. Consequently, since the organization of the department it has been concerned with the development and maintenance of defence production resources in Canada which can keep abreast of the changing needs of the armed forces and can also be expanded quickly on short notice.

This has meant, in many cases where military equipment of a specialized nature was involved, that Canadian industry has been asked to create important new facilities, both large and small, and to acquire the technical skills needed for the production of highly complex equipment. It has also meant that for the more commonplace type of supply we either limit our invitations to tender to Canadian suppliers or grant a reasonable preference to goods of Canadian manufacture over any competing goods of foreign manufacture.
Where the development or expansion of Canadian industrial capacity has been necessary we encourage industry to undertake this job of expansion through private investment as far as possible, since the equipment demands of the services affect almost every part of industry and the total cost of providing all the equipment needed for defence production would be prohibitive. However, we are continuing in appropriate cases to encourage defence industries to organize and expand their capacities through the granting of accelerated depreciation allowances. Where industry is unwilling or financially unable to provide the necessary facilities, because of the likelihood that there would be little, if any, residual value on completion of a defence project, direct capital assistance is available.
It is my general policy, therefore, to develop and protect Canadian defence production capabilities to the greatest extent possible. I might point out that the need for development of new capacity is much less now than it was seven years ago. However, we are conscious that the continuous change in defence equipment requires that the existing industrial base be maintained in up to date condition and adapted from time to time to new requirements.
Then, there is the recommendation that the department distribute purchases as broadly as possible in Canada. I have dealt with this before. The next recommendation was that the department use the maximum Canadian equipment and parts where possible. I dealt with this point in my statement this morning.
Then, there is the recommendation that technical assistance presently offered to larger corporations should also be made available to smaller Canadian companies. I understand that this refers to the capital assistance program of the department, and I would assure members that we do not differentiate between large and small companies in considering requests for assistance of this sort. I might explain that the purpose of such assistance is to provide machine tools and other production facilities needed for the production of 66968-9-361J
Supply-Defence Production defence equipment where there is no commercial application for the plant and equipment involved. It so happens that the greatest need for capital assistance is experienced in the aircraft program and as a result has affected the major aircraft manufacturers more than any other company. This, however, is not because they are large but because of the nature of the work in which they are engaged. All possible requirements are given equal consideration regardless of the size of the contractor.
Then, there is a recommendation that Canadian plants should be provided every opportunity to tender on defence contracts. I have dealt with that in my statement this morning. The next recommendation is that development contracts should be available for tooling and product development. I have not heard any questions on this point.
May I ask the minister whether there is any defence production in Canada, apart from mutual aid, for NATO countries other than the United States?
One example I would give the Leader of the Opposition is the manufacture of torpedoes for the United Kingdom. This is one example which comes to my mind.
Can the minister tell us if there are other examples, other commonwealth countries, for example?
There are other firms in Canada which have contracts for other countries, but I am sorry to tell the hon. member for Trinity that I do not have these figures or names of the countries available here.
I understood the minister to say we were manufacturing torpedoes for the United Kingdom.
Yes.
What contract does Britain now have under which they are manufacturing military equipment for us?
There is some in the shipbuilding industry; tank-automotives; weapons; ammunition and explosives; electronics and communication equipment and some aircraft equipment.
Does the minister have any idea of the dollar volume on an annual basis?

Here I have the net value
of Canadian government defence contracts placed in the United Kingdom by defence production on behalf of the Department of National Defence. The contracts placed amounted to $6,093,000, of which $1,921,000 was for aircraft; $147,000 for ships; $1,091,000

Supply-Defence Production for tank-automotive; ammunition and explosives, $237,000; electronics and communication equipment, $2,143,000; other equipment, $857,000. The value of expenditures on Canadian government defence contracts placed in the United Kingdom by the Department of Defence Production and Defence Construction Limited on behalf of the Department of National Defence amounted in 1958 to $13,157,000.
Would the minister say there had been any diversion of purchases from the United States to the United Kingdom?

I understand the hon. member for Trinity is quite serious, but I think he is fishing. I am sure that defence contracts were executed on behalf of the Department of National Defence, and it is rather difficult for this department to say we really diverted some of the trade. I would not want to make a statement to that effect because we fill any orders requested by the Department of National Defence.

I am really surprised that the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production have not made a little more effort in this regard, especially after checking back in Hansard and reading the words of the Minister of Finance as recorded on page 5523 of Hansard for June 29, 1956, where he says:
-express again regret that the department did not find it possible to make in the United Kingdom more of the purchases that it was unable to make in Canada and in that way assist the United Kingdom with its dollar problem in order that it might in turn purchase more of our products in this country.
With reference to the F-104 Lockheed Star-fighter, could the minister say he recommended the purchase of that aircraft to the cabinet defence committee?
It certainly is not the role of the Minister of Defence Production to recommend any aircraft to any department.

I am glad to hear that, Mr. Chairman, although from the words of the Minister of National Defence the other day we gathered the views of the Department of Defence Production had carried a considerable amount of weight, perhaps even an overwhelming proportion.
Mr. Chairman, the member is putting words in my mouth. I never said at any time that the opinions of defence production carried overwhelming influence.

The minister is quite right, he did not. He certainly led us to believe that they had been consulted and from that, 
and from the context in which he put it, we gathered that their views had been given overwhelming consideration.
Well, you were quite wrong.
I wonder if the Minister of Defence Production could tell us what the cost of tooling for the F-104 will be?
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but I have not the figures on tooling available here.
Perhaps the minister could get those figures for us. In the meantime, would he tell us where the tooling will be done?

Mr. Chairman, all I can say is that all the tooling which is needed will be done in Canada, except as I mentioned, I think, in my statement this morning when I spoke about the engine, that there might be some very intricate parts too expensive to make tooling for. As I said before, 85 per cent of the parts of the engine will be made in Canada and the airframe will be practically all made in Canada. But the tooling will certainly all be done in Canada.
The tooling will be done in Canada. I wonder if the minister could tell us whether the West German government plans to do its own tooling at the same time for production in its own country?

Mr. Chairman, as for what the Germans are doing with their own manufacture I am at a loss to say. I am sure it is not expected that we should know what the German contract is with Lockheed. All we know is that there is a definite contract signed for the 66, and we will be making some parts here in Canada for these 66 F-104G's which have been bought from Lockheed by the German government.

I wonder if the minister will continue with his comments on the estimates committee report of last year with reference to the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation and the contents of the committee report concerning the organization and management of that corporation, and also the final recommendation which dealt with the advisability of employing an independent business consultant to examine one or more of the crown companies. The report says that on completion of this review the government should then decide whether a further examination of the remaining crown companies is desired. I wonder what progress has been made in that direction?

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the hon. member for York-Scarborough would mind if we continued with the balance of the

questions with regard to the F-104 and then he can pursue this other point if he wishes.

Mr. Chairman, was that question directed at me? It is a question of who is interrupting whom. I had a question going here which was interrupted by somebody on that side before I had an opportunity to continue it.
The hon. member may as well go ahead now he is awake.

In reply to the hon. member for York-Scarborough, consideration was given to the recommendation of the committee and we are preparing plans for a management consultant with regard to crown assets which is before the government at this time. The reason it was not done before was because of the excess amount of work in front of crown assets through the disposal of a lot of property during the late fall and winter months; but the plan, as I say, for a management consultant is before the government and the president of crown assets is perfectly in agreement with the suggestion which has been made.
I wonder if the minister would tell us if any arrangements have been made, or what attempt has been made to work out a production sharing arrangement with the West German government?
There is no arrangement worked out with the West German government as yet, none whatsoever.
Is there any intention on the part of the minister to work out a production sharing arrangement with the Germans?
Yes. I think it will be a difficult situation, and I do not know what prospects there are of any success; but if there is any chance I am sure we will see what can be done.

Mr. Chairman, I gathered from the minister's statement this morning that arrangements have already been made to share the payment to the manufacturers in the United States of the design and engineering costs with the German government. As the minister said this morning, the design and engineering costs associated with the alteration to the F-104G model which Canada must pay will be up to 7 per cent, plus a licence fee and royalties. That means there will be an additional charge of $28 million. Could the minister say how much of that $28 million is Canada's share of the design and engineering costs of the remodelling, and how much is the licence fee and the royalties to be paid to this United States company for the privilege of manufacturing in Canada an airplane for Atlantic defence?
Supply-Defence Production

The licence, Mr. Chairman, as the Leader of the Opposition knows, is the straight, ordinary fee of $3 million for all the aircraft. The royalty is $20,000 per aircraft; and the development of the F-104G is $14 million for the production and the alteration.
Is the minister saying that it will cost Canada $14 million for her share in altering this plane to make the F-104G suitable for the use it is intended for?
We each pay the same amount, both West Germany and Canada.
Is it true that the West German government is using the same mark of this aircraft, the G model, which is proposed to be used by the Canadian government?
Yes, West Germany is using the F-104G.

Could the minister say what share the United States manufacturer is paying of the cost of development and design? I gather we are paying a certain percentage of the cost of the redesigning and redeveloping; what share does the United States company pay?

I do not want to be exact, Mr. Chairman, about this, but my understanding is that it is $28 million. Germany is paying $14 million and we are paying $14 million to make the F-104G. If other planes are sold there will be a reduction in those costs. This is what I understand is the fact.
Is it the case that if the United States air force should use this redeveloped and redesigned plane, the F-104G, our share of the cost of the redevelopment and redesigning goes down?
Yes.

As far as the minister's first statement is concerned that the 7 per cent is to be shared by Germany, he said, and I am quoting from his statement, a copy of which he gave me this morning:
The remaining 7 per cent-
That is, 7 per cent of the total cost of the contract for Canada, which is $400 million.
-represents payments to the original manufacturers for Canada's share of the design and engineering costs-
Yes. You have the licence, and then our share of the production. You have the royalties and licence of the engine, which comes to roughly 7 per cent of the contract.

When the minister said that the Canadian share will be further reduced

Supply-Defence Production if the aircraft is adopted by other countries, he included in "other countries" the United
States?
Yes.
Because the redesigning and redevelopment is now purely for Canada and West Germany?
That is right.
Is the engineering for the F-104G complete?
The engineering is complete.
Is a model being made of the F-104G and, if so, does tooling exist for it or is it being made by hand as a prototype?

The tooling is ready. Only parts of these planes are being developed. The whole plane is not being redeveloped. The tooling is there. Under the contract they have to have 66 planes for West Germany. Parts of the tooling are going to be sent to the manufacturer in Canada for the manufacture of certain parts of the aircraft.

The minister says only parts of it are being redeveloped, and that is true but the Minister of National Defence has told us that the airframe is being altered, the wings are being altered, and the fire control and electronic equipment are being altered. These are very serious and comprehensive changes. They may be compared to the process of making a light truck into a heavy truck. You start out by putting on heavier tires and wheels, and then you find you need a heavier axle. Then, if you drive across a ploughed field you find that your frame twists like a pretzel. Then you have to have a new frame, which leads to a new drive shaft and, perhaps, a new engine. Sometimes these minor modifications can become substantial operations.
If I may, I will refer to the Minister of National Defence and pose a question based on information given to us by him. We should like to know what makes these planes easier to modify by way of comparison than Canadian interceptors, because the Minister of National Defence told us the other day that the F-104G was selected as the most suitable after more than 20 types of British, United States and European aircraft, including our own interceptors had been evaluated by the R.C.A.F. As reported in Hansard at page 5352, he told the committee:
Such aircraft were developed essentially as fighter or interceptor aircraft, and were designed to engage hostile bombers at great heights. The requirements for a strike reconnaissance aircraft do not demand long range and great height, but do call for the ability to fly fast at low altitudes. The two requirements are not compatible.
[Mr. Fearson.l
What the minister is telling us today is that he is taking the very type of plane which the Minister of National Defence told us could not be reworked into a low altitude strike reconnaissance aircraft, and proposing to modify it, and do that cheaply because there will not be many modifications involved

Surely the hon. member realizes that in defence production work we talk about production, the awarding of these contracts and their execution, but I am unable to enter into details now regarding the technical side of the manufacture of these aircraft.

I thought the Minister of Defence Production might have had that information since the Minister of National Defence did not. Perhaps the minister would be able to tell us how long his officials have been working with Lockheed in working out the terms of this proposed contract.

The officials of my department' have had several meetings with the Lockheed company, as with other aircraft manufacturers. The date of the first meetings goes back, I think, to November. But the real negotiations are going on now in California. One of my officials has just returned, having been down there for over a week. But there have been several conversations and meetings with Lockheed company officials during the winter months, as with other companies.

I am glad to hear that negotiations go back that far. There seems to be some confusion on this point, because on March 5, 1959 when the Minister of National Defence was speaking about the Messer-schmidt contract he said he had no detailed information on the subject-it was a matter between the government of West Germany and the government of the United States. That was in March. Last week, in the debate on the estimates of the Department of National Defence, he gave us a different impression, namely that the question had been under serious consideration at least as far back as January. There seems to be something inconsistent about those statements.
Nothing inconsistent.

Perhaps the Minister of
Defence Production would tell us if he thinks it is efficient for both the governments of West Germany and of Canada to build up completely from scratch to manufacture limited numbers of these planes?
I cannot give an answer to that question. It is a technical question.

The Prime Minister told us on March 3 of this year, and I quote from page 1553, that we would work with the United States in the same way as the United States and Canada work with all the other countries of NATO on the continent of Europe-
-to the end that in the spirit of unity and a common dedication of purpose we shall be able to assure to this and future generations the freedom which we inherited.
We have heard a great many speeches about production sharing and working together in the western world within the NATO alliance to find the most efficient and cheapest means of producing defence requirements, yet here is a perfect example of two NATO countries, both presumably embarking on the production of very limited quantities of the F-104G completely failing to carry out in practice the high-sounding declarations which were made in those speeches. I understand, of course, that these aircraft are not for the same purpose; that in the case of West Germany they are getting the plane as an interceptor and plan to use the Fiat as a strike reconnaissance plane, whereas we are presumably intending to use the F-104G as a strike reconnaissance plane. Notwithstanding this difference, this would seem to be an excellent opportunity for the governments of Canada and West Germany to get together to work out a system of cooperative defence sharing in order to reduce the cost to the taxpayers of both countries. I am surprised and disappointed to learn from the Minister of Defence Production that no effort has been made in this direction. Now perhaps the minister would explain to the committee what is meant by a competition for the production of this plane in Canada.

We are asking for proposals -tenders if you will. As the hon. member for Trinity knows, we have here three major manufacturers. We want to see that this work is distributed in the centres where there are possibilities; I think it is important that no new industry should arise for the manufacture of new components, but that we should offer encouragement to the companies which have worked in this field in past years.

I am a little confused. The minister said "tenders, if you will" and yet he referred in the same sentence to "proposals". Are these proposals to be made in a form designated by the Department of Defence Production so that they may be evaluated properly, and so that there will be no question whatever as to the relative merits of these proposals?
Supply-Defence Production

The three companies have already had a meeting with officials of my department, and the same instructions have been given to the three companies. The same instructions were given and will continue to be given by my department, and they will be the same for three of them.

Do the three companies have complete sets of engineering drawings of the aircraft and its component parts and do they know precisely what tooling they will have to do and to what extent assistance will be available from the Department of Defence Production and the Lockheed corporation?
I should inform the hon. member for Trinity of the fact that officials of the three companies are today in Burbank, California, obtaining the information they require from the corporation.
I hope they have a nice trip and that the weather is good down there.
Oh, oh.
I know that hon. gentlemen opposite want to get home as soon as they can and so do we but we are not going to be bullied by a big government majority.
We will go on shifts and keep you here until December.

Can the minister assure us that the competition will be so arranged that upon examination the committee would be satisfied that the submissions have been made on the basis of quality with no room for interpretation or interpolation in assessing the merits or evaluating the proposal?
I hope that the hon. member for Trinity is not interested only in quality and that he is interested also in price. Price and quality are two important factors.
I thought that was implied in my question.

Mr. Chairman, would the minister be kind enough to let us know what is the proportion of contracts which have been awarded without tenders being called? I appreciate that he would not have that information at his fingertips but I am agreeable to receiving it when he has it available either in writing or verbally at the conclusion of his estimates.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was interested in the question asked by the hon. member for York-Scar-borough. When the committee examined the estimates of the Department of Defence
5694	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Defence Production Production last year I believe we were unsatisfied with the methods used for procurement and with many other phases of the department. I was pleased about the questions he asked and not at all satisfied with the answers.
The need for implementing the recommendations of the committee are highlighted by an article entitled "A Story of Waste on the Mid-Canada Line", which appeared in Saturday Night, issue of March 14, which article was written by Arnold Edinborough. He explains that the magazine made an investigation into the cost of the mid-Canada line. It cost the Canadian taxpayer something over one-quarter of a billion dollars. The author points out that this project consisted of building 102 separate sites across northern Canada and involved the handling of over 200,000 tons of material. A project of this magnitude would assume the drawing up of a contract document with a managing director. In this instance it was the Bell Telephone company. The contract was not drawn up until nearly the end of the construction phase. As a result of this there was no clearly defined authority for responsibility as between the Department of National Defence, which was the actual customer for the line, the Department of Defence Production, which was the procurement agency, Defence Construction Limited, responsible for the actual construction, and the management contractor who should have had over-all authority. The article sets out the following as being required for this project:
(1)	The signal and radio equipment cost approximately $34,500,000.
(2)	Transportation to get this equipment into the line cost $42 million.
(3)	Cost of housing and servicing that equipment was $107 million.
The author points out that the simple conclusion from these figures is that the cost of construction and transportation as opposed to the cost of equipment was in a ratio of 4 to 1. This indicates that this was not necessarily the type of company that should have been the management director of this job. The article cites many instances of outright waste simply because the company was qualified in the fields of construction and transportation. The article continues:
From Winisk on March 17, 1956, an Inspection report informed the engineer in charge that "the piles (for the harbour) received since the beginning of February form a good part of the last purchase by the prime contractor. They are eastern pine and of a very poor quality. There is evidence that they may be poles rejected by the Ontario Hydro company in that they bear the Ontario Hydro stamp and are dated 1953. Many have spiral checks, are badly distorted, and show signs of having been cut from a burnt timber stand. Breakage is between 30 and 40 per cent, tending toward the latter".

There are many other instances which if the article is accurate reveal that the company was unqualified, or if qualified, botched the job which would not have happened if the recommendations of the committee had been implemented. I continue:
The most dramatic example of this waste of money both to feed and lodge skilled men (as well as to pay their wages for doing nothing) is contained in a memo to the E.C.A.F. from the cost inspection and audit division, querying the claim of a construction company, whose contract was for the antennae and transmission lines.
Says the CIAD: "We would like to draw your attention to the considerable number of charges for room and board supplied to the contractor's employees in Montreal in varying periods which are described as "waiting time pending transit to site". Some of these periods are two and three weeks in length and total to a considerable sum of money. These waiting periods occur not only at the time of hire but are charged as well for periods in between engagement at sites".
The CIAD might well question this particular account in which 22 men were listed as putting in waiting time to a total of $3,490.41. One man alone had hotel bills of $1,066.98-this apart from his normal pay. In this particular instance, in fact, waiting time accounted for 6 per cent of the total contractor's claim for that area.
The author mentions other projects that were mishandled and points out the need for managerial service to put the contracts on a sound basis. A section of the article entitled "How the Money was Wasted" reads as follows:
A gravel crusher was shipped into Hudson's bay from Toronto. It stayed on Bear island all summer and was freighted back from Halifax after the St. Lawrence freeze-up. It never turned a wheel in all this time.
Two landing craft were bought from the British navy so that stores could be unloaded from their bow doors on the beach at Winisk. When they arrived in Canada, these LCT's had their bow doors welded up. As a result a small harbour had to be constructed at cost of well over a quarter of a million dollars.
One technician had hotel bills for over $1,000 while waiting to go from Montreal into the construction area.
Thousands of small wooden slabs to be used as mounts for switches were individually wrapped and sealed before being freighted in.
The article goes on to point out what this waste amounted to, and what it could have bought. The article goes on:
The over-run on the mid-Canada line was in the neighbourhood of $30 million.
This could buy 2,500 medium-cost three-bedroom homes. Pay the total salaries for all members of parliament and the cabinet for over 10 years. Pay the total fees and maintenance costs of all four years for 5,000 young Canadians going through university. Buy six Arrow aircraft. Mean a charge of over $5 out of the taxes of every member of Canada's labour force.
I think this reporter in doing a survey of some of the waste that took place under procurement methods by this and previous governments has given an indication that

something is wrong with the system that is being used by defence production.
I think it is well understood that the members of the committee last year were not at all satisfied that the department had done the job that they should have done in removing some of these loopholes that the committee recommended be removed. I think the type of waste that is taking place under one contract of $30 million is so important that we would be well advised to hire outside managerial consultants. No matter how busy the department appears to be, the questions and recommendations which were raised by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo warrant immediate consideration, and the waste of $30 million should be looked into and no excuse should be accepted.

I want to ask the minister one or two questions about the answer he gave to a question of mine which appeared in Hansard of June 3 with regard to procurement in the Atlantic provinces. I understand the minister made some statement about that this afternoon when I was at the broadcasting committee, and if he has answered any particular question I raised I apologize to him because I am not trying to hold up the committee at all. The minister did give the impression at the end of that statement, although I do not think he exactly said it, that there had been a very substantial increase in last year-that is to say, since March 31, 1958-in the amount of procurement in the Atlantic provinces. The minister will perhaps recall that in the famous Atlantic resolutions of 1957, which were endorsed unanimously by all the Tory candidates in the Atlantic provinces and which were published under the name of the Conservative party, the first part of the second of those resolutions reads-this was one of the things they pledged themselves to:
Decentralization by placing a more equitable share of defence contract expenditures within the Atlantic provinces.
What I want to find out from the minister is, first of all, what was the dollar increase in 1958-59 over 1957-58, in the total defence purchases in the Atlantic provinces? I will give the questions all at once. Second, what proportion of that increase was on construction; what proportion was on shipbuilding or ship repairing for both years, and what proportion of it was on the procurement of an industrial character; that is to say, things that were bought from industrial plants because that is what it was promised would be increased. Of course, I have the minister's answer. Although I do not question the factual accuracy of the answer, I think it
Supply-Defence Production was very misleading indeed because obviously, of course, expenditures on construction are not contributing to the decentralization, as was promised by the government. Neither, of course, are expenditures on shipbuilding and ship repairing unless indeed the government is deliberately diverting that work from some other part of the country to the Atlantic provinces. Of course, if that is done deliberately at a higher cost I wish the minister would answer that question also. Perhaps the minister would like to answer those questions; then, I may not have any others.

I certainly cannot answer all of the questions that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked me just now; I have not this breakdown. I have a prepared statement on the defence work in the Atlantic provinces. I shall be pleased to give him this report. I have not got at hand a breakdown of the question asked.
Perhaps the minister should not bother giving that statement now. What I am interested in is answers to the specific questions.
I have no objection.
Perhaps it can be given at a later stage.
I will get the answers for the hon. gentleman.

The other thing I would like to ask the minister is that if at the same time he would indicate which of the contracts let in the year 1958-59 were for entirely new projects initiated by the present government and which were merely a continuation of projects that had been started by the previous administration. That is very important, because if any attempt is made to show that there has been any progress in bringing about this industrial decentralization, which we were promised would be the result of the change of government, we have to know whether it is something new or merely, as I suspect most of it is, a continuation of the projects that were started by the previous government.
I will obtain this information for the hon. gentleman.

speechtext:
The matter which has been raised by the Saturday Night reporter, pointing out this vast waste of money, warrants some consideration by the department and some answer. Certainly this must have been investigated. These charges have been made publicly and there must have been some investigation.
