The mid-Canada early warning line is basically a detection system, which is supported by a transcontinental communication network. The whole line is constructed over terrain which, from the accessibility and climatic point of view, is the most difficult in Canada. The problems of construction, transportation, communications and manning were of such magnitude as to require an unprecedented degree of effort and team work by the Department of National Defence, the Department of Defence Production, Defence Construction Limited, and Canadian industry.
It was decided to proceed with the project in two phases. Phase I was to include a technical study and report including an estimated cost for the complete project. Phase II known as the implementation phase,


involved the complete engineering, procurement, transportation, construction and installation of the entire system.
It was realized that the construction of a communication system of this magnitude demanded that the basic planning and systems engineering be of the highest order and excellence. As it was to be built across all provinces of Canada, it was obvious that advantage should be taken of the local knowledge in the various provinces.
After a great deal of study and consultation with the armed forces, industry and experts in the communications field, it was established to the satisfaction of the Department of Defence Production that the employment of one company in the commercial communications field to manage the contract was the most efficient way to carry out a project of this magnitude and complexity. The techniques used to operate the system are almost entirely those of communications theory and practice. The major contribution to reliability rests with the ability of the communication system to carry the necessary warning data from each detection station to its appropriate sector station where after screening the combined information it is passed to air defence command.
The organization in Canada which most satisfactorily filled the requirement was the trans-Canada telephone system. This system comprises all the major provincial and commercial telephone operating companies and was set up primarily to allow a smooth and efficiently reliable transcontinental system to be achieved. It is because of this that the Department of Defence Production considered the trans-Canada telephone system the best organization to fulfill the requirement for co-ordinated systems engineering, planning, provincial know-how and the means to bring a large body of experienced and proven communication people together.
The exact relatonship between the contractor and the crown took some time to define because the original plan envisaged delegating almost complete control to the management contractor. This was dropped in favour of one where the Department of Defence Production performed its normal procurement functions, Defence Construction Limited was responsible for construction contracts and the RCAF acted as design authority. Under this plan the management contractor would co-ordinate all aspects of the engineering, construction and installation of the system.
Every contract placed by the Department of Defence Production or Defence Construction Limited, contained a clause stating that the requirement was a portion of an over-all project which was being co-ordinated by the

trans-Canada telephone system (represented by the Bell Telephone Co. of Canada as management contractor) and stating that the management contractor would act under the control and direction of the Minister of Defence Production as agent of Her Majesty in the supervision of the contract.
An executive committee to speak for the deputy ministers of the departments of government directly concerned with the building of the mid-Canada line and to act as a "clearing house" for complex problems was formed in November 1954. The management contractor was a member of this committee. The committee met monthly for 17 regular meetings in Ottawa and for many special meetings in Ottawa and at mid-Canada line sites. Most problems were settled at these meetings despite the varied opinions and convictions of individual committee members concerning technical and managerial matters.
Although the tentative program developed by the systems engineering group (RCAF) in June 1954 envisaged the completion of the line by the end of 1957, there was an urgent necessity for rapid and continuous improvement in the North American air defence system which accelerated the project so that the line could be in essentially full operation by January 1, 1957. Portions of the mid-Canada line were in operation as early as September 1956. The line came into operation sector by sector progressively, proceeding from west to east along the line. A report, dated January 8, 1957, indicated the detection equipment working from Winisk on the west side of James bay to Dawson creek with some sections of the balance of the line also in operation. Provisional acceptance tests and interim operational tests continued through the spring and late summer of 1957. Some deficiencies such as tower clean up, antennae alignment and modifications to the north-south Doppler detection equipment were carried over into the maintenance contracts.
Under the terms of his contract, the management contractor submitted "Forecasts of Expenditures" quarterly. The first was submitted in May of 1955 with an overall estimate of approximately 169 million. This figure included approximately 16.7 million for management function. This estimate remained unchanged in the management contractor's quarterly forecasts until August 1956 when the management contractor revised the estimate upwards by 10 million to 179 million. At the insistence of the R.C.A.F. and the executive committee, the management contractor immediately undertook a complete review of the mid-Canada line costs and submitted early in October an estimate of approximately $206 million. This estimate was
Supply-Defence Production discussed at the executive committee meeting of October 15, 1956 and additional breakdowns of cost estimates and reasons for change were requested. It was also agreed that an estimate should be made to provide for interim maintenance costs prior to the effective date of the maintenance contract. This further	review	was undertaken	by	the
management contractor and completed by the end of October, part of which was made with the assistance of the systems engineering group personnel. This study established a figure of 203.4 million for the construction phase with 6.4 million for interim maintenance.
Cost estimates were under constant review from this point on, with the highest estimate of $230	million	for construction	and	$9.8million for interim maintenance appearing in March 1957 quarterly review. The present estimate	of cost	inclusive of interim maintenance	is $228	million.
Only a few of the reasons for upward revision in the over-all costs are outlined here for your information. Construction costs increased as a result of additional buildings (185 in place of 120); the size of the buildings increased by 31 per cent in cubic content; two additional rearward scatter sites and three additional DDSs were added; special harbour work at Winisk had to be undertaken; additional airstrips had to be constructed; there was a fire loss at Knob Lake; and extra foundations as well as access roads had to be built. The increase in sites resulted in an increase in the number of main towers, as well as an increase in electronic equipment, diesels, domestic furnishings and transportation costs. The original estimates did not provide for the purchase of helicopters or the procurement of scows, barges, and other lightering equipment for use in Hudson Bay. The original estimate for transportation did not provide funds for rental of civilian helicopters as it was anticipated that RCAF could supply all helicopter support. The early target completion date necessitated airfreight of urgently required equipment including the Dorman diesels airlifted from England. Later estimates included equipment to be left on site for RCAF use during the maintenance of the line and was estimated to provide two years' maintenance of spares. This also included fire-fighting equipment, heavy construction equipment, laundry equipment, furniture, kitchen and mess equipment as well as spares and tools to be put into stock for replacement and repair.
Shipping conditions in the Hudson bay were far from ideal. Cargo returned to Montreal by ship urgently required for winter construction had to be airlifted. A record cold

Supply-Defence Production winter on the eastern half of the line caused extremely high consumption of fuel for heating and construction operations and required airlift of fuel not previously planned.
The stress of this project from the first was one of urgency as to time and this unquestionably contributed to higher costs. It was generally recognized that this approach would result in heavier costs than would be the case in a normally spaced program. To meet the date, it was necessary to work during the extremely difficult annual freeze-up and break-up periods when efficiency of operation drops markedly.
It must be accepted that a project of this magnitude undertaken, as it was, on a "crash" basis would be fraught with differences of opinions, both technical and administrative, and problems of an almost insurmountable nature. The decision to hire a contractor to take over completely the detailed responsibilities, perform the management function including over-all co-ordination, technical assistance and detailed design as required was intended to relieve the RCAF design authority, Defence Construction Limited and the Department of Defence Production of details for which no staff was available. The hopes of the government agencies, that the detailed responsibilities would be taken over by the management contractor, were not entirely fulfilled. It should be pointed out, however, that the work was carried out at a time when the entire construction and shipping industries were struggling to cope with some of the heaviest demands in their history. It is reasonable, therefore, to conclude that the project could not always progress in the most efficient and desired manner.
While those who were close to the project may remember it chiefly for the difficulties which had to be overcome collectively, it is generally agreed by the members of the executive committee that the construction of the mid-Canada line was a truly remarkable achievement, and it accomplished its objectives in spite of an unavoidable but nevertheless complicated administrative control. These controls are of course essential in all projects involving large expenditures of public funds.

Question
The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Was Canada a party to the 1949 road traffic convention?
2.	If so, what negotiations have been conducted with the provinces concerning the possibility of Canada ratifying this convention?
3.	By what means have such negotiations been conducted?
4.	What attitude has each of the provinces expressed to the ratification of this convention?
5.	Does it appear likely that Canada will be able in the near future to ratify this convention?
Answer by:	Hon. Howard C. Green
(Secretary of State for External Affairs):
1.	No.
2.	In 1949 provinces were informed of the forthcoming UN conference on road and motor transport and of its possible implications for Canada. After the conference, their views were requested on the possibility of ratification by Canada of the convention on road traffic. In 1956 they were asked whether they would be willing to bring their legislation into line with the provisions of the convention. They were also consulted
in 1953 and in 1957 concerning detailed questions of implementation in the matter of the licensing of drivers.
3.	By correspondence, in most cases between the lieutenant governor of the province concerned and the secretary or the under secretary of state.
4.	Not all the provinces have replied to the government's inquiries. One province has suggested that provinces should not be asked to comment on this problem separately, as decisions of this nature should be arrived at at a conference of all the provinces. Two provinces have expressed their lack of interest, and two provinces have stated that they are working to achieve uniformity of provincial legislation by other means. Two provinces have suggested that ratification of the convention, or discussion of this possibility, would be of little value. Two provinces have replied without commenting on the desirability of ratification.
No province has expressed interest in the possibility of Canadian ratification. One province has said that none of the provisions of the convention conflict with its own legislation, but no other province has given a substantive reply to our enquiry of 1956.
5.	After completing a review of the inconvenience caused to motorists abroad by failure to ratify the convention, the government will decide whether a further approach should be made to the provinces.
